official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security; Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (DOJ's Middle District of Tennessee brought and prosecuted the underlying case)
offense_category: Vindictive Prosecution -- Bringing Criminal Charges in Retaliation for a Successful Civil Lawsuit Against the Government, a Due Process Violation a Federal Judge Found This Case Actually Met
incident_summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national living in Maryland with a U.S.-citizen wife and child, had been granted protection from deportation under a 2019 immigration court order after a judge found he faced danger from gang targeting of his family. In March 2025, Trump administration officials deported him to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison anyway, in violation of that court order -- an error the administration itself later acknowledged in litigation while resisting court orders to facilitate his return. Abrego Garcia sued and won, forcing the government to return him to the United States by June 2025. DHS then issued an April 2025 press release describing a 'bombshell investigative report' alleging Abrego Garcia was a suspected human trafficker, based on a 2022 Tennessee traffic stop in which he was found driving with nine passengers and released with only a warning at the time. Prosecutors in the Middle District of Tennessee subsequently charged him with human smuggling and conspiracy to commit human smuggling. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly touted the indictment at a press conference, saying 'This is what American justice looks like.' U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw Jr. first found in October 2025 that Abrego Garcia may have been charged out of prosecutorial vindictiveness, writing that 'the Government had a significant stake in retaliating against Abrego's success' in his deportation lawsuit, and ordered a hearing on the question. In May 2026, Judge Crenshaw dismissed the case outright, finding 'presumptive vindictiveness' and writing that 'absent Abrego's successful lawsuit challenging his removal to El Salvador, the Government would not have brought this prosecution,' concluding 'the evidence before this court sadly reflects an abuse of prosecuting power.' The Justice Department vowed to appeal the dismissal.

The individual sued the government and won, forcing his return to the United States

Criminal charges were subsequently filed against the same individual, based on conduct (a 2022 traffic stop) that had not previously resulted in charges despite being known to law enforcement at the time

A federal judge -- not merely the defendant or his advocates -- independently found the prosecution was likely brought in retaliation for the successful lawsuit, using the legal standard of 'presumptive vindictiveness,' and ultimately dismissed the case on that basis

Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0495): this investigation's roots predate the November 2025 grand jury by several months, and trace to DNI Tulsi Gabbard's July 2025 declassification of documents she said showed Obama-era officials fabricated the 2016 Russia-interference intelligence assessment, plus a related criminal referral to DOJ. Retired CIA counterintelligence chief Susan Miller, a co-author of the original 2017 assessment, publicly rejected that claim on July 26, 2025, saying the finding that Russia sought to help Trump was based on verified intelligence, not the Steele dossier or a fabricated narrative. Prosecutors recommended felony charges against Abbott and several of its executives under the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act. Tysen Duva, the DOJ Criminal Division's assistant attorney general, supported pursuing the felony charges, but was overruled by senior DOJ leadership -- now under Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- which ordered the criminal investigation closed. DOJ instead pursued a civil False Claims Act settlement, stating this was 'the best mechanism to achieve accountability, deterrence and protection of the public' and noting the settlement included a 'significant' monetary penalty, though it did not specify the amount in the reporting reviewed. Sen. Adam Schiff opened an inquiry into the decision, writing to DOJ: 'Under your management, DOJ does not consider a case involving deadly risks to medically sensitive infants, after a recommendation of a felony charge, to be worthy of criminal prosecution,' and demanding an explanation for why prosecutors' advice was rejected. Abbott is represented by Kirkland & Ellis, one of the law firms that struck a deal with the White House providing pro-bono legal services to pro-Trump causes -- the same firm documented elsewhere in this tracker's entry on DOJ's subpoenas of law firms over Boris Epshteyn communications.

incident_summary: In an April 2026 NBC News interview, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's former personal defense attorney -- was asked about a communication in which Trump had publicly implored then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to indict several of his political enemies. Blanche described Trump as 'my boss' and characterized the investigations into Trump's political opponents as receiving 'outsized focus' only because 'they involve individuals that the president has had significant issues' with -- not because of their share of DOJ's actual caseload. Separately, Blanche suggested prosecutors could continue pursuing cases against a target even after a grand jury declines to indict, rather than treating a declined indictment as the matter's end -- a posture legal commentators noted lacks the customary 'no true bill' safeguard requiring disclosure when a grand jury has already rejected a case before it is re-presented elsewhere. The interview came as Blanche's own nomination for permanent Attorney General faced a contested Senate confirmation process.

incident_summary: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0232): the deals underlying these later subpoenas originated over a year earlier. Starting around February 2025, Trump used executive orders to strip lawyers at firms he viewed as hostile -- including firms that had represented his adversaries or investigated him -- of security clearances, government contracts, and building access. Rather than negotiating with government attorneys, targeted firms instead cut deals directly with Boris Epshteyn, Trump's personal lawyer, who by April 2025 had extracted commitments of close to $1 billion in free legal services for Trump-aligned causes plus changes to hiring practices, according to the Wall Street Journal; firms reported reaching these deals include Paul, Weiss, Skadden, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, Kirkland & Ellis, Latham & Watkins, A&O Shearman, and Simpson Thacher & Bartlett. The subpoenas were disclosed in the ABA's ongoing lawsuit alleging its members face harm from the administration's law-firm policy; DOJ's stated position was that the ABA should seek this information from its own members or the firms rather than from the White House directly, while simultaneously invoking executive privilege to withhold Epshteyn's communications from direct disclosure, framing them as confidential presidential advice.

offense_category: Potential quid-pro-quo clemency arrangement / abuse of prosecutorial discretion in connection with a convicted co-conspirator's cooperation, prison classification, and possible pardon (relevant concerns: 18 U.S.C. Sec. 201-adjacent bribery/gratuity principles do not directly apply to clemency itself, but the sequence raises conflict-of-interest and equal-justice concerns given Blanche's prior personal representation of Trump); not charged, no formal investigation into Blanche's own conduct identified in sourcing reviewed
incident_summary: Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0502): on July 18, 2025, amid mounting pressure over DOJ's withheld Epstein files, DOJ under AG Bondi asked the Southern District of New York to unseal grand jury materials from Maxwell's criminal case; a parallel DOJ motion to unseal grand jury materials in the original Florida Epstein criminal case was denied on July 23, 2025 by U.S. District Judge Robin Rosenberg, who found binding 11th Circuit precedent left the court's "hands are tied" and that the government's own arguments supplied "no exceptions" to grand jury secrecy -- a rejection DOJ itself effectively conceded, per Rosenberg's order. Amid mounting public and congressional criticism over DOJ's refusal to release the full Epstein files, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's own former personal defense attorney -- personally interviewed Ghislaine Maxwell, Jeffrey Epstein's convicted co-conspirator serving 20 years for sex trafficking, over two days (July 24-25, 2025) in Tallahassee, Florida, under a grant of limited/proffer immunity; Trump publicly said he had ordered the DOJ to 'release all credible evidence.' Maxwell's attorney said she 'answered every single question' and had been cooperating '100%.' Roughly a week after the interview, on August 1, 2025, Maxwell was quietly transferred from a low-security facility to FPC Bryan, Texas -- one of only three minimum-security federal prison camps in the country, ordinarily reserved for low-risk, often white-collar offenders -- a transfer multiple former federal prison officials called 'highly unusual' for a convicted sex offender. Victims were given until August 5, 2025 to submit letters on DOJ's SDNY unsealing motion; two anonymous victims did so. One, in a letter reported by CNN on August 4, called the push "political warfare" that shields powerful men while ignoring survivors and wrote that the government's continued handling of the matter was "eating at me day after day." A second, in a letter reported August 10, objected specifically to what she called Maxwell's impending "public legitimization," separately criticizing Maxwell's prison transfer just described, DOJ's private meetings with her, and clemency speculation, and accused the administration of retraumatizing survivors by moving to unseal without consulting them first. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer -- the same judge who later denied Maxwell's habeas petition, described below -- denied DOJ's unsealing bid in a scathing 31-page order, calling the government's central premise that the materials would reveal meaningful new information about Epstein's or Maxwell's crimes "demonstrably false," and separately faulting DOJ for failing to notify Epstein's and Maxwell's victims of the request in advance -- the same notification failure the victims' own letters had already flagged. On August 31, 2025 (the transcript covers the July 24-25 interviews), DOJ released the interview transcript (263 pages for day one, 66 for day two) and audio; in it, Maxwell said she 'never saw' Trump 'in any inappropriate setting' and disputed aspects of her own conviction, casting doubt on accuser Virginia Giuffre's allegations -- prompting Giuffre's family to say DOJ had given Maxwell 'a platform to rewrite history.' Maxwell's attorney has since said publicly that Maxwell wants clemency from Trump in exchange for her cooperation; Trump has called clemency 'allowed' while denying plans to grant it. Congress responded with bipartisan opposition: the House passed H.Res.635 expressing that Maxwell should not receive a pardon, commutation, or other clemency, and Democracy Forward separately sued DOJ and the FBI on August 19, 2025 to force release of communications about the investigation, including any Epstein-Trump correspondence. Maxwell's own legal position has weakened since: the Supreme Court declined to hear her direct appeal on October 6, 2025. Reps. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia sent DOJ/BOP inquiry letters on October 30, 2025 seeking answers about her treatment; on November 9, 2025, NBC News reported on Maxwell's own emails from her first months at FPC Bryan, obtained by the House Judiciary Committee, in which she called herself "much much happier" and "safe," while separate Wall Street Journal reporting documented additional perks (dormitory meal delivery, late-night workouts, priority shower access) and inmates alleging retaliation, including one transfer, for discussing Maxwell with reporters. On November 10, 2025, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin disclosed that a whistleblower had come forward describing extensive special treatment FPC Bryan's warden was arranging for Maxwell: customized meals delivered to her cell, private visitor meetings in a cordoned-off area with refreshments, visitors permitted to bring computers (described as unprecedented), the warden personally handling her documents and correspondence, after-hours private exercise time in staff-only areas, and access to a service-dog-in-training for recreation that other inmates and staff were not normally permitted to touch. Raskin said the same whistleblower reported Maxwell was actively preparing a formal commutation application for submission to Trump with the warden's assistance. Raskin publicly demanded written answers from Trump on the extent of any clemency discussions and requested Blanche testify publicly before the Committee; no response from Trump, Blanche, or the Bureau of Prisons was identified in reporting reviewed. In February 2026 she invoked the Fifth Amendment rather than testify before the House Oversight Committee after months of defying its subpoena; and on August 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer denied her self-represented habeas corpus petition in a 67-page opinion calling her claims 'meritless' and warning that further appeals would not be considered made in good faith.

official: Todd Blanche, Deputy Attorney General
offense_category: Weaponizing the Federal Clemency Process for Political Loyalty -- firing DOJ's career Pardon Attorney for declining a personal favor for a Trump ally, then installing a political appointee who has used the office to fast-track clemency for MAGA-aligned figures
incident_summary: Elizabeth Oyer, DOJ's career Pardon Attorney since 2022, was fired on March 7, 2025 -- two days after Todd Blanche was confirmed as Deputy Attorney General. Oyer later testified (including before the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 16, 2026, during Blanche's own confirmation hearing to become Attorney General) that Blanche's office had asked her to recommend restoring gun rights to actor Mel Gibson, who lost that right after a 2011 misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction and who has a personal relationship with President Trump; Gibson's attorneys had written directly to senior DOJ officials citing a special appointment he had received from Trump. When Oyer declined and was pressed to reconsider, she was fired without any stated reason in a termination letter signed by Blanche. On May 14, 2025, Trump appointed Edward 'Ed' Martin Jr. -- previously interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, known for openly blending Trump's political goals with DOJ's clemency function -- as the new Pardon Attorney. Within two weeks of Martin's appointment, Trump had pardoned more than two dozen MAGA-aligned loyalists and wealthy donors, including Culpeper County, Virginia Sheriff Scott Jenkins, convicted in December 2024 on federal bribery charges in a 'cash-for-badges' scheme and sentenced to 10 years; Martin posted 'No MAGA left behind' after the Jenkins pardon. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0359): the same late-May 2025 wave -- within two weeks of Martin's appointment, as this entry already frames it -- also included reality-TV stars Todd and Julie Chrisley, pardoned May 28, 2025 after a 2022 conviction for defrauding banks of more than $30 million and evading federal taxes; their daughter Savannah, a Trump-aligned media figure and RNC speaker, had publicly and personally lobbied for their release, and Trump called Savannah directly to tell her the pardons were coming. The same wave commuted the sentence of Larry Hoover, a Chicago gang leader (Gangster Disciples) serving multiple life sentences for conspiracy and drug-trafficking convictions -- a notable outlier from the wave's otherwise white-collar/MAGA-loyalist pattern, since Hoover's case is neither a fraud conviction nor an obvious political-donor connection. Martin went on to organize symbolic pardons for participants in the 2020 fake-elector scheme and to grant clemency or pardons to a number of Trump-connected officials and campaign donors. ProPublica reporting found no comparable path forward for ordinary clemency applicants under the restructured office. A June 17, 2025 House Judiciary Committee Democrats analysis, led by Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, quantified the pattern's scope beyond named individual examples: Trump's pardons and commutations -- more than 1,600 recipients, including white-collar and fraud convictions well beyond the MAGA-loyalist cases above -- had eliminated roughly $1.3 billion in restitution and fines owed to crime victims and taxpayers. (Martin's later removal from DOJ's Weaponization Working Group over a separate grand-jury-leak finding is documented in this database's ed-martin-grand-jury-leak-2026.json entry -- a related but factually distinct episode from the clemency-favoritism pattern this entry covers.) Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0478): on December 3, 2025, Trump pardoned Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX) and his wife, ending a sitting Democratic member of Congress's active federal prosecution mid-case -- a materially different scenario from this entry's other examples, which involved already-convicted or symbolic beneficiaries rather than a pending indictment against a sitting lawmaker. Cuellar and his wife had been indicted in 2024 on 12 counts of bribery, conspiracy, and money laundering centered on an alleged roughly $600,000 in bribes from Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank; two Foreign Agents Registration Act-related counts had already been narrowed under a separate Trump-driven policy sharply limiting FARA prosecutions before the pardon voided the remaining charges entirely. Cuellar's response undercuts any 'reciprocal loyalty' framing of the pardon: he announced he would run for re-election as a Democrat, prompting Trump to publicly call the decision 'a lack of LOYALTY' on social media -- itself evidence that the administration frames pardons as transactions expecting political fealty in return, consistent with this entry's core thesis. Government watchdog group CREW sued for records on the pardon's origin, and Cuellar continued to face a separate House Ethics Committee investigation (opened May 2024, reauthorized July 2025) unaffected by the federal pardon.

incident_summary: Boeing's 2021 deferred prosecution agreement over the fatal 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths combined) was found violated after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout revived scrutiny of the company's compliance record, putting Boeing back on track for prosecution on the underlying fraud-conspiracy charge -- deceiving FAA regulators about a flight-control system (MCAS) implicated in both crashes. Judge Reed O'Connor rejected an initial revised plea-deal version in December 2024. Reuters reported May 17, 2025 that crash victims' families were preparing to formally object to a new tentative nonprosecution agreement the Trump-era DOJ had reached with Boeing, which would let the company avoid a felony conviction. The DOJ formally announced the agreement May 23, 2025, and the parties filed the final written Non-Prosecution Agreement on May 29, 2025: Boeing avoids trial and any felony conviction; pays a $487.2 million criminal fine (crediting $243.6 million already paid under the 2021 agreement); contributes $444.5 million to a new victims'-families compensation fund; and commits at least $445 million more to compliance, safety, and quality programs -- a total 'pay or invest' commitment DOJ said exceeds $1.1 billion. Boeing must retain a DOJ-selected Independent Compliance Consultant and cooperate with authorities for two years, but the agreement does not include the court-supervised independent monitoring the 2021 deal's compliance-oversight regime nominally provided. Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote Attorney General Bondi May 22, 2025 questioning the deal's adequacy. Victims' families -- relatives of those killed in both crashes -- formally objected, calling it 'a step backward' from real accountability. On November 6, 2025, Judge O'Connor granted DOJ's motion to dismiss the underlying criminal case, approving the agreement, but wrote that the families opposing it 'are correct' that it 'fails to secure the necessary accountability to ensure the safety of the flying public' and 'disregards the need for Boeing to be subject to independent monitoring' -- concluding, however, that he lacked legal authority to override DOJ's charging decision even though he disagreed the dismissal served the public interest. Families' attorneys said they planned to appeal to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Concentrating Sole Certification Authority Over an Accelerated Capital-Appeals Process in the Attorney General, on an Honor-System Basis -- a proposed rule, not yet finalized; a due-process/executive-power-concentration accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: DOJ proposed a rule making it easier for states to obtain certification for an accelerated federal review process for death penalty cases under a 1996 federal law (the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act's Chapter 154 opt-in provisions). Attorney General Pam Bondi argued that regulations implemented during the Obama and Biden administrations had improperly prevented states from using the law's fast-track option, which -- once a state is certified -- cuts a death-sentenced prisoner's window to file a federal habeas petition from one year to 180 days and requires federal courts to prioritize capital habeas petitions over all non-capital cases. Under the proposal, the certification decision (whether a state's system for providing competent post-conviction defense counsel meets the law's requirements) rests solely with the Attorney General, based substantially on the certifying state's own representations about the quality of its post-conviction counsel system -- a process critics, including the Death Penalty Information Center, describe as effectively an honor system that does not independently verify defense-counsel quality or consider opposing views before certification. Bloomberg reported the change is part of the Trump administration's broader push to expand use of the federal death penalty. Critics quoted by Davis Vanguard and other outlets warned the accelerated timeline and reliance on state self-certification increase the risk of executing people without adequate review of wrongful-conviction claims.

The certification process, as proposed, relies substantially on the certifying state's own self-reported representations rather than independent review, per the Death Penalty Information Center's analysis
The rule change is explicitly framed by DOJ's own head as part of a broader push to expand use of capital punishment, rather than a neutral procedural adjustment

offense_category: Wholesale Deprioritization of Federal Criminal Enforcement Outside Immigration -- a prosecutorial-discretion and resource-allocation accountability claim, not an allegation that declining any specific case was individually improper
incident_summary: A ProPublica investigation, examining two decades of DOJ case-declination data, found DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi closed more than 23,000 criminal investigations without prosecution in the first six months of the administration -- including cases involving terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drug trafficking, and environmental crimes -- while ramping up immigration prosecutions. The majority of the declined cases had been referred to DOJ by law enforcement agencies, including under prior administrations, whose investigators believed a federal crime may have been committed. February 2025 alone, covering the first weeks of Bondi's tenure, saw nearly 11,000 declinations -- the most in a single month since at least 2004, when comparable data begins, and far exceeding the prior monthly high of roughly 6,500 declinations set in September 2019 during Trump's first term. ProPublica's analysis found the increase was not attributable to a larger inherited caseload or increased referral volume from law enforcement, indicating a deliberate shift in prosecutorial priority rather than a passive resourcing effect.

The declined cases span multiple serious categories (terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drugs, environmental crimes), not a single narrow category
The February 2025 monthly declination total (~11,000) is the highest in at least two decades of comparable data, exceeding even the prior high recorded during Trump's first term

ProPublica's analysis ruled out caseload inheritance or referral-volume increases as explanations, supporting a characterization of the decline as a deliberate prioritization shift toward immigration enforcement

offense_category: Federal Indictment of a Civil Rights Attorney Over a Corrected Misstatement, Amid a Broader DOJ Push Against Transgender-Care Litigation and Providers
incident_summary: Three Alabama federal district judges, in an inquiry beginning in 2022 (predating this administration), examined whether Lambda Legal attorney Carl Charles and other counsel had engaged in 'judge shopping' while challenging Alabama's ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender youth -- specifically, whether Charles called the chambers of a different judge to request the case be assigned to her as a related matter. Judge Burke found Charles had intentionally been dishonest when he initially denied making that call, though Charles corrected the statement himself within minutes, under oath, according to Mother Jones's reporting. In September 2025, under the Trump administration's DOJ, federal prosecutors secured a criminal indictment against Charles for making a false statement before a court; the indictment was unsealed September 8, 2025 in federal court in Montgomery, Alabama, and Charles pleaded not guilty. The prosecution came amid a broader DOJ push under the Trump administration to investigate providers and legal advocates involved in gender-affirming care for transgender youth -- a pattern documented elsewhere in this database (trump-gender-affirming-care-eo-2025.json, doj-nyu-langone-trans-care-subpoena-2026.json). Lambda Legal called the indictment 'an outrageous act of governmental overreach' and said it stood behind Charles; the New York City Bar Association and other advocacy and legal organizations publicly condemned the indictment as disproportionate and intimidating toward civil rights lawyers generally.

incident_summary: In recent weeks before mid-July 2025 reporting, DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi fired several career prosecutors, investigators, and at least one administrator who had worked on U.S. Capitol riot (January 6) prosecutions, without prior notice or stated cause (CBS News, July 2025). incident_summary: Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0346): the eventual staffing collapse documented below followed an earlier procedural change to the section's authority. The Washington Post reported May 17, 2025 that DOJ was considering, and Bloomberg Law reported was actively weighing, ending the longstanding requirement that federal prosecutors obtain the Public Integrity Section's approval before bringing corruption charges against members of Congress and other elected officials, and ending the requirement that U.S. Attorney's offices consult the section's career lawyers during such investigations -- a Watergate-era safeguard designed to prevent politically motivated prosecutions by letting career, non-political attorneys review case merits before politically appointed U.S. Attorneys could indict. That review-authority requirement was in fact suspended, freeing political appointees to prosecute public officials without the section's traditional gatekeeping review. In late March 2026, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche circulated a memo proposing to reorganize the section further, reassigning most of its remaining personnel out to individual U.S. Attorney's offices -- the same reorganization that produced the two-attorney staffing collapse described below. Under Attorney General Pam Bondi, DOJ's Public Integrity Section -- the unit responsible for prosecuting public corruption by federal, state, and local officials -- was reduced from roughly 36-40 full-time attorneys handling 175-200 open matters at the start of the second Trump term to just two attorneys overseeing about 20 remaining investigations by May 2026, per current and former DOJ officials. The section, the oldest of its kind since its 1976 creation, has never been this small. The staffing cut coincided with parallel rollbacks elsewhere in DOJ's anti-corruption infrastructure: a pause in enforcing the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act against U.S. executives who bribe foreign officials, disbanding of an FBI squad devoted to investigating congressional misconduct, disbanding of a task force pursuing Russian oligarchs' assets, and a pullback in enforcing the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Over the same period, Trump pardoned at least 15 people who had been charged with or convicted of public corruption, including political allies and supporters. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse sent DOJ a formal oversight letter demanding answers on the section's dismantling. Bondi left DOJ in April 2026; Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense attorney, became acting Attorney General and has not publicly moved to restore the section's staffing.

incident_summary: ICE agent Jonathan Ross fatally shot Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, in south Minneapolis on January 7, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge; Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said video evidence did not appear to support DHS's account that Good was using her SUV to run over an agent. Rather than pursuing a standard investigation of Ross's use of deadly force, top DOJ officials pressured the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota to instead investigate Good's widow, Becca Good, reportedly examining any ties she might have to activist groups. An FBI Minneapolis field-office supervisor who attempted to investigate Ross himself was pressured to step away from that investigation and subsequently resigned. In response, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson -- the office's lead prosecutor on the high-profile Feeding Our Future fraud case, which had charged 78 people and secured 58 convictions -- resigned along with five colleagues (Harry Jacobs, Melinda Williams, Thomas Calhoun-Lopez, Ruth Schneider, and Tom Hollenhurst) in mid-January 2026, citing DOJ's reluctance to investigate the agent and the push to investigate Good's widow instead. Eight additional assistant U.S. attorneys, including civil division chief Ana Voss, left the office in early February 2026, citing continued frustration with how DOJ was handling both the Good case and the separate fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0792): the resignations extended beyond the Minneapolis U.S. Attorney's Office to DOJ headquarters itself. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon personally decided not to open a civil-rights (excessive-force) investigation into Ross's shooting -- a decision legal experts called highly unusual, noting DOJ's own manual calls for Civil Rights Division involvement in cases designated as a matter of 'national interest.' In response, at least six leaders of the Civil Rights Division's criminal section resigned in protest, a separate, headquarters-level wave distinct from the Minneapolis resignations already documented above; some contemporaneous reporting put the total Minneapolis-office departures as high as 13 attorneys rather than the more specifically-sourced 6-plus-8 figures already documented here, a discrepancy this entry flags rather than resolves. DOJ instead treated the case as a potential assault on a federal officer, with prosecutors reportedly pressured to scrutinize Good's own conduct and her spouse rather than Ross's use of force, despite video evidence Mayor Frey said didn't support the official account. This fits a broader documented pattern: Wired reported ICE agents have fatally shot at least 25 people since 2015 with no criminal indictments, while a separate Fox 9 Minneapolis analysis found 59 ICE shooting investigations produced not a single indicted agent -- outlets differ on the exact shooting/fatality count, but agree no ICE agent has been criminally indicted for an on-duty shooting.

incident_summary: On February 10, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order, 'Pausing Foreign Corrupt Practices Act Enforcement to Further American Economic and National Security,' directing Attorney General Pam Bondi to halt new FCPA investigations and enforcement actions for 180 days and review existing matters -- the first pause of FCPA enforcement since the statute's 1977 passage. Bondi had already signaled the shift days earlier: on February 5, 2025, the day of her swearing-in, she issued a memorandum redirecting DOJ's corporate-enforcement priorities away from certain corporate crimes toward foreign bribery specifically tied to transnational criminal organizations and cartels. Pilgrim's Pride, a poultry company that pleaded guilty to price-fixing in 2021 and is controlled by Brazilian billionaire brothers Wesley and Joesley Batista -- who separately admitted to and paid record fines for bribery under Brazil's own anti-corruption law in a case tied to the same conduct area the FCPA targets -- was the single largest donor to Trump's 2025 inauguration, contributing $5 million, reported April 22, 2025. Ethics watchdogs raised concerns that a major donor with the Batista brothers' bribery history benefited from timing that coincided with the administration pausing the very federal law most directly relevant to their past conduct. DOJ ended the formal pause on June 9, 2025, when Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued guidelines resuming FCPA enforcement with a narrower focus -- prioritizing cases touching U.S. economic/national-security interests, transnational criminal organizations and cartels, and individual (rather than corporate) misconduct. FCPA tracking firms recorded the lowest level of publicly announced enforcement activity since formal tracking began in 2010 during and immediately after the pause. Update 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0344): Reuters reported May 19, 2025 that Sen. Elizabeth Warren sent a letter to JBS -- Pilgrim's Pride's Brazilian parent company -- demanding it explain whether it or Pilgrim's Pride communicated with Trump or his team about either the $5 million inaugural donation or a separate, long-delayed SEC approval for JBS's own dual-listing on the New York Stock Exchange, which had been approved just two days after a public FEC filing revealed Pilgrim's Pride as the inauguration's largest donor. Warren's letter also noted DOJ had two ongoing civil investigations into Pilgrim's Pride at the time, concerning its payment practices toward contract farmers and antitrust matters -- separate from, but concurrent with, the FCPA-pause concern already documented above. JBS completed its NYSE debut June 13, 2025, roughly six months after the donation. No source reviewed confirmed whether JBS or Pilgrim's Pride ever responded substantively to Warren's letter, nor whether the SEC's own approval timeline was in fact influenced by the donation, as distinct from the appearance of the timing itself. Update 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0435): the Miami Herald reported July 11, 2025 that Bondi herself, not just a donor, had a direct undisclosed financial tie to a second beneficiary of the pause. Financial disclosures showed Bondi earned more than $200,000 from a law firm for representing Pfizer -- the sole client she listed for that work -- yet she did not disclose this Pfizer representation on her Senate confirmation questionnaire or in her testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Pfizer's own SEC filings had disclosed an ongoing DOJ investigation into potential FCPA violations tied to its China and Mexico operations; its next annual report, filed roughly three weeks after Bondi took office, no longer referenced that DOJ investigation. incident_summary: Alina Habba, a former personal defense attorney for Trump, was installed as acting/interim U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0490), the root cause of the disqualification ruling below: when Habba's interim term expired, New Jersey's own federal district judges exercised their statutory authority to appoint a replacement, choosing career prosecutor Desiree Grace rather than extending Habba. Trump responded by firing Grace and withdrawing Habba's own pending nomination as permanent U.S. Attorney, keeping Habba in the post without the judges' authorization -- Judge Matthew Brann's later 77-page order found Habba had 'exercised the functions and duties of the office... without lawful authority since July 1, 2025' as a direct result. The dispute first surfaced publicly when defendants facing narcotics charges argued in court that prosecutors could not proceed against them without a validly appointed U.S. Attorney in charge, triggering a wave of paused trials, postponed hearings, and delayed guilty pleas across the District of New Jersey as the authority question worked through the courts; Brann ultimately declined to dismiss those defendants' cases outright, instead disqualifying Habba from participating in their cases and any other ongoing matters. McIver pleaded not guilty and argued Habba's unlawful appointment should void the indictment; the Third Circuit's December 1, 2025 ruling disqualifying Habba did not retroactively dismiss the case, and an August 2026 appeals ruling allowed two of the three charges to proceed to trial despite the authority dispute. McIver's prosecution was part of a broader wave of federal and local officials facing arrest, assault, or charges in connection with immigration-enforcement protests and oversight activity in mid-2025, including Sen. Alex Padilla, NYC Comptroller Brad Lander, and Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan (separately charged with obstruction for allegedly helping an undocumented defendant evade arrest in her courtroom) -- a pattern Time magazine's June 2025 reporting characterized as officials facing consequences for opposing the administration's immigration crackdown. A federal judge ruled her appointment unlawful, finding the arrangement violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and, separately, that a structure allowing the administration to unilaterally extend her tenure past normal limits amounted to 'a unilateral appointment in violation of the Constitution's Appointments Clause.' An appeals court upheld the disqualification ruling, and Habba resigned in December 2025. A federal judge ruled this arrangement was also unlawful, finding DOJ had unlawfully split the power of the U.S. Attorney's office among the three-person team specifically to route around the earlier disqualification ruling. In the most recent escalation, the same judge (per AP News) threw a government prosecutor out of court and ordered the top officials running the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office to testify under oath, condemning DOJ's leadership structure there as 'chaotic' and potentially unconstitutional.

incident_summary: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memorandum rescinding Attorney General Merrick Garland's July 2021 policy, which had shielded journalists from compelled testimony and record seizures in leak investigations after it was revealed the first Trump administration had secretly obtained records from at least nine journalists. Bondi's memo authorizes prosecutors to more readily seek subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants directed at journalists and news organizations to compel records and testimony related to leak investigations, provided such measures are approved by DOJ leadership, narrowly tailored, and preceded by advance notice to the journalist where feasible. incident_summary: Abigail (Gail) Slater, Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ's Antitrust Division, was forced out in February 2026 after roughly a year leading the division, during which she pursued aggressive antitrust enforcement. Friction with the White House had been building for months: round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0461: CBS News reported July 17, 2025 that Slater had already drawn criticism from colleagues and business leaders while leading active cases against Capital One, Apple, Google, and others, including friction over her office's handling of merger reviews -- Bondi's chief of staff Chad Mizelle had overruled her to accept a Hewlett Packard Enterprise/Juniper Networks merger settlement DOJ officials were confident was weaker than what the government could have won at trial. HPE had retained lobbyists with ties to the Trump White House to push the settlement through; Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison later moved to intervene in the federal court's Tunney Act review of the settlement, and House Judiciary Committee Democrats opened a probe into whether DOJ had ceded to lobbyists over its own antitrust experts' advice. Business leaders were reportedly unhappy after Slater warned them not to engage with the administration through Trump-aligned lobbyists and consultants seeking to influence pending antitrust matters; some administration officials defended her as principled and appropriately distrustful of well-connected allies attempting to sway confidential legal decisions. In December 2025, Trump issued a 'full and unconditional pardon' for Oak View Group co-founder Tim Leiweke, who had been indicted by Slater's own division earlier in 2025 -- undercutting an active enforcement action from within her own department. She had also lost the confidence of AG Bondi and Deputy AG Blanche, with a source telling reporters officials felt new leadership was needed to advance the President's agenda; a separate travel-rules dispute (an unauthorized trip to a Paris conference) led DOJ to cut off Slater's government credit card access. Slater suggested in a public post that she was leaving voluntarily, but CNN's sourcing characterized the departure as a firing. Bondi publicly thanked Slater for her service; DOJ named Omeed Assefi acting antitrust chief. House Judiciary Democrats sent a formal letter to Bondi regarding the Antitrust Division following Slater's departure.

incident_summary: On July 11, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi fired Joseph Tirrell, the career director of DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office, in a four-sentence termination letter that gave no reason. Tirrell had spent nearly 20 years at the department and had led the ethics office since 2023, reviewing and approving financial disclosures, recusals, and conflict-of-interest waivers for DOJ leadership including Bondi herself, Deputy AG Todd Blanche, and FBI Director Kash Patel. Tirrell's portfolio had also included advising then-Special Counsel Jack Smith on ethics matters during Smith's prosecutions of Trump, including approving roughly $140,000 in free legal fees Smith received from a major Washington law firm. Tirrell was fired the same day Bondi dismissed at least 20 other DOJ employees with ties to Smith's prosecutions team, as part of a broader purge. Tirrell, along with two other fired former DOJ officials (Michael M. Gordon and Patricia A. Hartman), filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia seeking immediate reinstatement and back pay. The lawsuit noted that fired federal employees would normally be able to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board, but that the board had been left without a quorum after Trump removed one of its members -- leaving the plaintiffs without the administrative appeal process Congress designed for exactly this situation.

official: Emil Bove, Judge, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit (was Acting Deputy Attorney General when the conduct described occurred; the Senate confirmed him to a lifetime Third Circuit seat 50-49 on July 29, 2025, and he was sworn in September 2, 2025)
offense_category: Ordering Dismissal of a Pending Federal Corruption Indictment in Exchange for a Sitting Official's Cooperation on Unrelated Policy Priorities -- a federal judge found the arrangement carried the appearance of an improper quid pro quo; addressed here as an institutional-integrity and prosecutorial-independence matter rather than a criminal charge against Bove
incident_summary: New York City Mayor Eric Adams had been federally indicted on charges including bribery, wire fraud, and illegal foreign campaign contributions. On February 10, 2025, acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove ordered federal prosecutors to move to dismiss the case without prejudice -- preserving DOJ's ability to revive the charges later -- citing concerns that the prosecution would interfere with Adams's ability to assist the administration's immigration-enforcement priorities and with his reelection campaign, rather than any evidentiary or legal weakness in the case. The order triggered a cascade of resignations: Acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Danielle Sassoon, who had held the post only three weeks, resigned rather than comply, writing that Adams's attorneys had effectively proposed a quid pro quo in a meeting with DOJ -- that Adams would cooperate with the administration's enforcement priorities only if the indictment were dropped. The then-acting chief of DOJ's Public Integrity Section and a deputy assistant attorney general also resigned rather than sign the dismissal motion. U.S. District Judge Dale Ho ultimately dismissed the case on April 2, 2025 -- but with prejudice, permanently barring its revival, rejecting DOJ's request to dismiss without prejudice. Judge Ho wrote that 'everything here smacks of a bargain: dismissal of the indictment in exchange for immigration policy concessions,' finding it 'disturbing' that a public official might receive favorable prosecutorial treatment contingent on advancing the administration's policy goals, and that dismissing without prejudice would create 'the unavoidable perception that the Mayor's freedom depends on his ability to carry out the immigration enforcement priorities of the administration.' Senators Whitehouse and Blumenthal later filed ethics complaints against Bove with DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility and New York's attorney grievance body. A June 2025 NBC News analysis situated the episode within a broader four-month pattern of DOJ anti-corruption rollback under the new administration, including the Inspectors General purge and a halt to foreign-bribery enforcement documented elsewhere in this database.
elements_required: Adams faced a pending federal corruption indictment with specific charges (bribery, wire fraud, illegal foreign contributions)
DOJ leadership ordered dismissal explicitly citing the case's interference with the administration's policy priorities and Adams's reelection, not any evidentiary weakness

Multiple senior career prosecutors, including the Senate-unconfirmed but sworn-in acting U.S. Attorney, resigned rather than carry out the order, with the most senior resignation letter alleging DOJ leadership had been offered a functional quid pro quo
The presiding federal judge independently found, in a written opinion, that the arrangement carried the appearance of exchanging prosecutorial leniency for policy cooperation
The judge dismissed with prejudice specifically to eliminate the leverage a without-prejudice dismissal would have given the administration over Adams going forward

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (institutional attribution -- a Marine Corps 250th-anniversary demonstration held under DoD auspices and attended by Hegseth and Vice President JD Vance; no specific individual was named in sourcing as personally authorizing the decision to fire live artillery over the highway)
offense_category: Authorizing Live Artillery Fire Directly Over a Major Public Interstate Highway for a Televised Political Spectacle, Resulting in a Malfunctioning Round Striking a State Patrol Vehicle
incident_summary: On October 19, 2025, the Marine Corps staged a live-fire demonstration at Camp Pendleton, California, commemorating the Corps' 250th anniversary and recorded for a future prime-time broadcast, attended by an estimated 15,000 invited guests including Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The demonstration included Marine forces moving from Navy ships offshore onto Pendleton's Red Beach, and howitzer artillery firing directly over Interstate 5 -- a major corridor between Los Angeles and San Diego, closed to traffic during the exercise -- intended to land far to the east in the base's Whiskey Impact Area. One M795 high-explosive round detonated prematurely, at an altitude of roughly 1,480 feet, scattering shrapnel onto the closed roadway that struck and damaged a California Highway Patrol vehicle and motorcycle; the patrol vehicle was part of Vice President Vance's own security detail. No injuries were reported. Military and police officials described firing live artillery directly over a public interstate as 'highly uncommon.' The day before the event, California Gov. Gavin Newsom called the demonstration 'dangerous' and 'unnecessary,' saying 'firing live rounds over a busy highway isn't just wrong -- it's dangerous,' and accused the administration of prioritizing spectacle over public safety; Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) countered that Newsom had improperly interfered with Marine Corps planning and staged 'a spiteful publicity stunt,' with his spokesperson dismissing media coverage as 'comic exaggerations.' Rep. Mike Levin led 26 House members and two senators in a formal letter demanding answers on who had authorized firing over the freeway and how the safety risk had been assessed beforehand; state Sen. Catherine Blakespear called the event 'posturing with militaristic bluster at the expense of the safety and well-being of the community.' A Marine Corps investigation, detailed in a 666-page report dated December 19, 2025, concluded there was 'no definitive answer' for why the round detonated early, characterized the malfunction as a 'one in a million' occurrence, and found no negligence or wrongdoing by Marine Corps personnel involved.
elements_required: DoD leadership authorized and staged a televised political-anniversary event that included firing live artillery munitions directly over an open, later-closed, major public interstate highway
A round malfunctioned and detonated over the highway, scattering shrapnel that struck a state law-enforcement vehicle assigned to protect the sitting Vice President

A state governor and dozens of members of Congress from both chambers formally characterized the underlying decision (not merely the malfunction) as reckless and demanded accountability for who authorized it

The military's own investigation, while finding no personnel negligence in the malfunction itself, could not identify why the round detonated early and did not address whether firing over a public highway was itself a sound safety decision

Chavez-DeRemer resigned as Labor Secretary on April 20, 2026 amid the mounting allegations -- the third member of Trump's Cabinet to leave within two months -- and, per reporting, falsely claimed a 'deep state' conspiracy was behind the scrutiny on her way out. offense_category: Repeated Policy Flip-Flopping on Classifying Swastikas and Nooses as Hate Symbols, Followed by an Actual Swastika Incident at a Recruit Training Center -- documents an institutional policy failure rather than any single official's criminal conduct
incident_summary: In November 2025, The Washington Post reported the Coast Guard would no longer classify swastikas and nooses as hate symbols under a new workplace-harassment policy, instead labeling them merely 'potentially divisive.' Within a day, the Coast Guard reversed course and said both would again be classified as hate symbols. Despite that public reversal, Commandant Adm. Kevin Lunday's order to maintain the hate-symbol classification was never actually incorporated into the policy for reasons that remain unclear, and the more lenient 'potentially divisive' language was allowed to take effect in mid-December 2025 despite objections from members of Congress. Facing renewed uproar, the Coast Guard deleted the downgraded language again on December 18, 2025, restoring the hate-symbol classification for a second time. Roughly two months later, on February 19-20, 2026, an instructor found a swastika hand-drawn on a bathroom wall at the Coast Guard's primary recruit training center in Cape May, New Jersey; Lunday personally flew to the base to address roughly 900 recruits and staff, condemning the symbol's use, and the Coast Guard referred the incident to its Investigative Service.

incident_summary: In late January 2025, a longtime DHS staffer -- who had worked at the department in various roles since the George W. Bush administration, including through Trump's first term -- accidentally added a journalist to a group email containing unclassified but sensitive details (timing and possible target-home addresses) about an upcoming ICE operation in the Denver area. She caught the error immediately, contacted the journalist, who agreed not to publish, and the operation proceeded without incident. Despite causing no operational harm, DHS placed her on administrative leave, opened an internal investigation, asked her to take a polygraph and surrender her cellphone (she declined both), and moved to revoke her security clearance -- a step that could end her career -- giving her 30 days to appeal. NBC News reported the story March 27, 2025, explicitly framing it as raising questions about unequal punishment for inadvertent leakers under the Trump administration. The same week, CNN reported that an unnamed defense official said of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's Signal chat disclosure of live Yemen strike-timing details to a group that inadvertently included a journalist: 'It is safe to say that anybody in uniform would be court-martialed for this.' Hegseth faced no discipline, criminal charge, or removal; the Pentagon Inspector General's eventual December 2025 final report (tracked separately in this database, see hegseth-signal-yemen-strike-2025-03.json) found DoD Instruction and Federal Records Act violations but no referral for prosecution.

offense_category: Due Process Violation -- Mass Termination of International Students' Legal Status Based on Unverified Law-Enforcement Database Entries, Without Notice or Judicial Review -- contested by DHS as a lawful national-security screening measure; a federal court has allowed the underlying due-process claims to proceed past a motion to dismiss
incident_summary: Starting around April 2025, DHS quietly launched what advocates and reporting termed a 'Student Criminal Alien Initiative': running roughly 1.3 million international students' names through the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database and terminating their SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) records -- effectively ending their lawful F-1 student status -- based on database hits, including for individuals who had never been charged with or convicted of a crime, only dismissed charges or minor police encounters. More than 4,700 students had their SEVIS records terminated in spring 2025 with no advance notice, no opportunity to respond, and no judicial review before the termination took effect, throwing their ability to remain enrolled, work, or stay in the country into immediate jeopardy. The Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, later joined by the American Association of University Professors and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on April 24, 2025 challenging the mass terminations as unlawful. Facing mounting litigation, DHS reactivated many terminated SEVIS records by late April 2025, restoring status for numerous affected students -- but did not concede the underlying policy was unlawful. On March 20, 2026, a federal judge largely denied the government's motion to dismiss the amended complaint, ruling the plaintiffs' due-process claims were not moot despite the reactivations because the challenged policy could reasonably recur, and that key issues -- including the legality of the mass revocations themselves -- remained unresolved. The case proceeded to discovery and merits litigation.

Affected students were not given advance notice or an opportunity to respond before termination took effect
A federal court found the resulting due-process claims sufficiently plausible to survive a motion to dismiss, rather than dismissing them as meritless
DHS's later reactivation of many records did not resolve or moot the underlying legal question of whether the initial mass-termination policy itself was lawful

incident_summary: DHS created a public website in December 2025 branding a list of roughly 25,000 arrested immigrants as the 'worst of the worst,' which Secretary Noem, DHS, and the White House heavily promoted on social media to justify the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement operations. After CNN presented its findings, a DHS spokesperson admitted the charges against hundreds of listed immigrants had been described incorrectly, attributing the errors to a 'glitch' the agency said it worked to fix, and the agency updated the site the same week. John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under the Obama administration, said the vast majority of so-called 'criminal aliens' are actually people charged with or convicted of traffic offenses, DUIs, and immigration-related offenses -- not violent or serious crime.

incident_summary: On January 23, 2025, Trump granted full pardons to 23 people convicted under the FACE Act (Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act) for blockading, invading, or harassing patients at reproductive-health clinics. incident_summary: A federal grand jury subpoena, confirmed by Arizona Senate President Warren Petersen, sought records related to the Arizona Senate's 2020 partisan 'audit' of Maricopa County's presidential election results -- an audit conducted by Cyber Ninjas and its subcontractor Cyfir that was widely discredited by election experts and produced results confirming Joe Biden's victory despite the audit's methodology. On March 7, 2026, an FBI agent removed more than three dozen hard drives and servers containing audit-related data and Cyfir subcontractor material from the Arizona Senate building; Petersen said he complied with the subpoena 'late last week.' The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors and Recorder's Office, who jointly administer the county's actual election operations, said they had not received subpoenas as of this reporting, though the Board said it would cooperate if one arrived. ProPublica reported election-security experts warned the seized audit records could be 'fatally flawed' as evidentiary material given the audit's own documented chain-of-custody and methodological problems. The subpoena follows and expands a broader federal pattern of using DOJ and FBI resources to re-examine 2020 election administration nearly six years after the election, after multiple independent audits, recounts, and court rulings in Arizona and nationally confirmed Biden's victory and found no evidence of the fraud the audit was commissioned to find.

This action is part of a documented, broader pattern of similar federal actions re-examining settled 2020 election results in other jurisdictions (Fulton County, Georgia poll-worker subpoena and ballot seizure)

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General / Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Non-Compliance With a Statutory Deadline for Epstein-File Disclosure, Alongside FBI Compilation of Unverified Allegations Against Other Prominent Figures -- raises accountability concerns distinct from any single named individual's conduct within the files themselves
incident_summary: The Epstein Files Transparency Act required DOJ to produce its Epstein/Maxwell-related files by December 19, 2025; DOJ said the process was delayed by the volume of material and the need to redact survivors' personal information. In the run-up to that deadline, Trump directed Bondi to open a new DOJ investigation into several of his political opponents' own links to Epstein; Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) publicly warned on November 15-18, 2025 that the new probe could function as a 'smokescreen' and 'last-ditch effort to prevent the release of the Epstein files,' explaining the underlying mechanism: 'If they have ongoing investigations in certain areas, those documents can't be released.' Former U.S. Attorney Barbara McQuade confirmed the legal basis for that concern, telling reporters that with a pending investigation, DOJ 'can assert executive privilege and try to prevent any more documents from being released.' Following the broadly-criticized rollout of a partial release ('The Epstein Files: Part 1') on February 27, 2025, Attorney General Bondi directed the FBI to deliver the complete files within 24 hours and ordered FBI Director Kash Patel to produce a comprehensive report within 14 days; as of the reporting reviewed, 74 days had passed since that directive without the report's release. Separately, as pressure mounted for full disclosure, CNN reported that FBI employees assembled a 21-slide internal presentation compiling what one employee described as 'salacious statements' about 13 prominent men in Epstein's orbit -- including Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, Prince Andrew (Mountbatten-Windsor), Leon Black, and Harvey Weinstein -- drawn from unverified allegations in the investigative files. DOJ ultimately released more than 3 million pages of documents and photos, including the 21-slide presentation itself, as part of the broader disclosure. On March 17, 2026, a House oversight committee subpoenaed Attorney General Bondi to testify about DOJ's handling of the Epstein files. Lawmakers from both parties alleged DOJ improperly redacted key information, failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act's disclosure requirements, and exposed sensitive details about survivors in the process. Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0448), filling an antecedent gap between the February 2025 'Part 1' rollout and the later disclosure fight: on July 9, 2025, FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino -- himself a former prominent Epstein-conspiracy podcaster before joining the administration -- had a heated clash with Bondi at the White House after Bondi publicly stated evidence confirmed Epstein died by suicide and that DOJ found no incriminating 'client list,' triggering backlash from both Democrats and Bongino's own MAGA-aligned base who felt they had been overpromised disclosures. Bongino told colleagues he was considering resigning and did not report to work the following Friday; Bondi separately accused him of leaking stories that blamed her for the public backlash. The Daily Beast reported Bongino left a subsequent West Wing meeting abruptly amid the tension. Reporting on Vice President JD Vance's role was less specific than other aspects of the episode -- Vance, along with Bongino and FBI Director Kash Patel, had each separately hinted at forthcoming disclosures that never materialized, but no sourcing reviewed confirmed Vance directly mediated between Bongino and Bondi. Bongino ultimately remained in his post through this episode. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0467: Sen. Dick Durbin, ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said July 18, 2025 that his office had received a protected FBI whistleblower disclosure alleging Bondi had roughly 1,000 FBI personnel placed on 24-hour shifts starting in March 2025 to comb through approximately 100,000 Epstein-related documents and flag any mention of Trump. Independent journalist Allison Gill separately reported anonymous FBI sources corroborating the account, saying they were directed to log Trump mentions in an Excel spreadsheet. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on July 21, 2025 that she was not aware of any effort to flag Trump's name and directed inquiries to the FBI. Durbin sent formal letters to DOJ leadership demanding an explanation, characterizing the deployment as a potential effort to identify and manage information about Trump within the files rather than the neutral, comprehensive review the department had publicly described; no source reviewed confirmed DOJ's or FBI's on-the-record response to the specific whistleblower allegation itself, distinct from the general denial reported through Leavitt.

offense_category: DOJ Criminal Subpoenas and FEMA/DHS Grant-Condition Demands Targeting Migrant Shelters and Their Funders Nationwide, Struck Down by a Federal Court as Unlawfully Coerced Immigration Enforcement
incident_summary: In March 2025, federal prosecutors served criminal subpoenas on at least three New York City hotels used as migrant shelters -- the Roosevelt Hotel, the Row NYC (Stewart Hotel), and the Hotel Chandler -- demanding the names, birth dates, and nationalities of residents, as well as the identities of the entities and individuals funding the shelter programs. In parallel, FEMA required recipients of its Shelter and Services Program grants nationwide to submit, within 30 days, lists of names and contact information for every migrant they had assisted, and required each recipient organization's executive officers to personally sign sworn affidavits attesting they had no knowledge or suspicion that anyone in their organization had violated federal human-smuggling law -- effectively conditioning continued disaster/shelter funding on self-incriminating attestations and mass data handover with no individualized suspicion. A coalition ultimately growing to roughly 20 states and the District of Columbia, led by Illinois, sued DHS, FEMA, and Secretary Kristi Noem in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (Illinois v. FEMA and the related Illinois v. Noem), arguing the administration was withholding congressionally appropriated emergency-preparedness funds unless states diverted resources to federal civil immigration enforcement. On September 24, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge William E. Smith granted the states summary judgment and permanently enjoined DHS and FEMA from enforcing the immigration-related conditions across 40 separate federal grant programs, finding the conditions unlawful.
elements_required: Federal agencies (DOJ, FEMA/DHS) demanded personal identifying data on migrants and shelter funders without individualized suspicion of wrongdoing
Grant recipients were required to sign sworn, potentially self-incriminating affidavits as a condition of receiving already-appropriated emergency-preparedness funding

A federal judge agreed and issued a permanent injunction, rather than the conditions being upheld or the case being dismissed

incident_summary: On July 4, 2025, a demonstration against Trump's mass-deportation push outside the Prairieland ICE detention center in Alvarado, Texas turned violent when former Marine reservist Benjamin Song shot and wounded a police officer who had just arrived at the scene. Nine defendants were tried together; a federal jury convicted eight of the nine on charges including rioting, weapons and explosives offenses, providing material support to terrorists, obstruction, and attempted murder of a law enforcement officer. Eight additional defendants separately pleaded guilty to one count of providing material support to terrorists. DOJ's own press releases branded the group 'Antifa Cell Members.' Sentences ranged widely: Song, convicted of attempted murder, received 100 years; other convicted defendants received sentences up to 60 years; those who pleaded guilty to the material-support count alone received 2-15 years. The Intercept reported one defendant received 30 years in part for transporting a box of antifascist zines, and Just Security separately analyzed how the terrorism statute used in the case is broadly enough defined that it could sweep in ordinary protest-adjacent conduct not involving violence. The trial featured testimony from more than 45 witnesses and over 210 exhibits across a 12-day proceeding.

incident_summary: Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0439), documenting the nationwide campaign's actual origin, which this entry had not previously dated: Attorney General Bondi issued a DOJ-wide memorandum on April 22, 2025 directing five enforcement priorities against pediatric gender-affirming care, including 'Enforcement of Laws Outlawing Female Genital Mutilation,' False Claims Act/FDCA investigations, and establishing a 'Federal and State Coalition Against Child Mutilation.' On July 9, 2025, DOJ announced it had issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics providing gender-affirming care to minors nationwide, without naming the recipients or their locations. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog cluster c0540): NBC News later identified the first named recipient in that wave -- Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) had received a subpoena dated June 11, 2025 (due July 9), demanding patient names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, addresses, and parent/guardian information for minors prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy, plus staff personnel files, patient intake procedures, and insurance billing codes for gender-affirming care; GLAD Law's Jennifer Levi called it turning 'doctor-patient confidentiality into government surveillance.' Neither DOJ nor CHOP responded to NBC's request for comment. The same week, the FTC held a workshop critical of pediatric trans healthcare featuring detransitioners and anti-trans activists; former FTC staff told NBC News the event was politically organized and exceeded the agency's normal jurisdiction, a parallel but institutionally separate action from DOJ's own subpoena campaign. DOJ subpoenaed Rhode Island Hospital (part of Brown University Health/Lifespan) for the birth dates, Social Security numbers, and addresses of every patient who received transgender care there over the prior five years, plus all documentation of adverse side effects in minor patients, assessments for puberty blockers or hormone therapy, patient intake forms, and guardian authorizations. On May 13-14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy (D.R.I.) blocked the subpoena, writing that DOJ had 'proven unworthy' of the trust ordinarily extended to federal prosecutors. McElroy wrote that the administration 'has publicly characterized gender-affirming care for minors as abuse, directed the justice department to bring its practice to an end, and celebrated when hospitals curtailed such programs as a result of this subpoena campaign' -- tying the subpoena to a stated political goal rather than a neutral investigative need. This is one of at least seven federal districts, including Massachusetts, where judges have now blocked DOJ subpoenas seeking hospitals' transgender-care patient records as part of the same nationwide campaign (see also this tracker's NYU Langone entry, a separate subpoena in the same campaign issued out of the Northern District of Texas). Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog cluster c0578): the Massachusetts block named above was U.S. District Judge Myong Joun's September 9, 2025 ruling quashing DOJ's subpoena to Boston Children's Hospital, which had sought patient records including Social Security numbers and home addresses, billing codes, communications with pharmaceutical manufacturers about puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones, and personnel files for all 2,000 of the hospital's employees. Judge Joun found the subpoena 'motivated only by bad faith,' writing that 'the Administration has been explicit about its disapproval of the transgender community and its aim to end GAC [gender-affirming care]' and that its true purpose was 'to interfere with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts' right to protect GAC within its borders, to harass and intimidate BCH to stop providing such care, and to dissuade patients from seeking such care.'

incident_summary: Tina Peters, the former Mesa County, Colorado clerk, was convicted in August 2024 on four felony counts for orchestrating unauthorized access to Mesa County's secured election system in 2021 as part of an effort to find evidence supporting Trump's false claims of 2020 election fraud, and was sentenced in October 2024 to nine years in state prison. On March 3, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice, in a court filing signed by Acting Assistant Attorney General Yaakov Roth, announced it would 'review' Peters's state conviction, questioning both the length of her sentence and Colorado's denial of bail pending her appeal as potentially 'arbitrary or unreasonable' -- without identifying any new evidence or legal defect in the state proceedings. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser publicly called the intervention a 'grotesque attempt to weaponize the rule of law.' At an April 23, 2025 federal hearing on Peters's bid for release, a federal attorney representing DOJ's position declined to explain, on the record, the department's actual reason for intervening in a completed state prosecution. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0304: Trump personally escalated the matter for the first time on May 5, 2025 in a Truth Social post directing DOJ to 'take all necessary action to help secure the release' of Peters, describing her as an 'innocent Political Prisoner' held 'hostage ... by the Democrats, for political reasons' and subjected to 'Cruel and Unusual Punishment,' and criticizing Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser by name for jailing her. Trump escalated the pressure further on August 21, 2025, threatening on social media, 'If she is not released, I am going to take harsh measures!!' The Federal Bureau of Prisons went further on November 12, 2025, formally pressing the Colorado Department of Corrections to transfer Peters into federal custody, with then-National Security Adviser Michael Flynn arguing she should be moved into federal custody as a potential witness in a 2020-election investigation; Colorado declined, stating such transfer requests must originate from the state itself, not other entities. A federal magistrate judge rejected Peters's bid for release on bond in December 2025, and she remained in state prison. Separately, on April 2, 2026, the Colorado Court of Appeals -- in a unanimous, 78-page opinion by Judge Ted Tow, reached independently of DOJ's intervention -- upheld Peters's underlying conviction but ordered her resentenced, finding the trial court's nine-year sentence was based 'in part on improper consideration of her exercise of her right to free speech' (the panel found the sentencing judge's comments suggested the term was meant partly to stop Peters from continuing to espouse views the court deemed 'damaging'). The same opinion rejected Peters's separate argument that a hypothetical presidential pardon could nullify her state conviction, holding the President has no pardon power over state offenses. The appeals court declined to rehear the case on April 23, 2026.

incident_summary: On April 18, 2025, ICE agents, FBI agents, and DEA agents entered Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan's courtroom to serve an administrative arrest warrant on Eduardo Flores-Ruiz, a noncitizen facing misdemeanor domestic-violence-related battery charges. Dugan allegedly directed Flores-Ruiz to leave through a back door normally reserved for jurors, allowing him to evade the agents. Dugan was arrested in late April 2025 and indicted by a federal grand jury on May 13, 2025, on one felony count of obstructing or impeding a federal proceeding and one misdemeanor count of concealing a person to prevent arrest. Dugan pleaded not guilty. Her defense moved to dismiss the case on judicial-immunity grounds, arguing that a judge's in-courtroom conduct is an official judicial act immune from criminal prosecution and that immunity should bar the case at the outset rather than being litigated later at trial. A magistrate judge recommended the case proceed, and U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman upheld that recommendation, rejecting the immunity argument and allowing the prosecution to continue. More than 150 former state and federal judges signed a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi criticizing the prosecution as an attempt to intimidate the judiciary.
