official: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Chairman, House Judiciary Committee
offense_category: Potential weaponization of congressional oversight and criminal-referral power against a former prosecutor over contested closed-door testimony -- not itself an executive-branch action, but a pattern of using investigative/referral power to pursue a perceived political adversary; the underlying perjury allegation, if pursued, would be a genuine 18 U.S.C. Sec. 1621 matter, but no charge has been filed
incident_summary: Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0748: on December 7, 2025, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan subpoenaed former Special Counsel Jack Smith for a closed-door deposition on December 17, 2025, seeking documents and testimony about Smith's prosecutions of Trump over the 2020 election and classified-documents cases. Smith's team said he would comply but noted he had previously (in October 2025) offered to testify publicly so lawmakers' questions and his answers would be visible to everyone; Jordan chose the closed-door format instead, telling Fox News it gave lawmakers and committee lawyers more time to question Smith. Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin criticized the closed-door format at the time, saying Republicans would 'spin, distort, and cherry-pick his remarks through press leaks.' The December 17 deposition proceeded in one-hour increments alternating between the two parties. On July 23, 2026 -- roughly seven months later -- Jordan issued a formal criminal referral asking DOJ to investigate Smith for 'willfully and intentionally false statements' made under oath at that deposition, specifically over Smith's testimony that neither he nor his team sought the contents of lawmakers' text messages, only toll (metadata) records. Records DOJ later produced showed Smith's team had obtained message content for communications involving 44 lawmakers -- but per Raskin's rebuttal, those came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, not from a subpoena directed at the lawmakers' own phones or messages, a factual distinction Raskin says Jordan's referral elides. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said DOJ takes such testimony seriously but made no commitment to prosecute; a criminal referral is a recommendation, not a charge. Smith's counsel called the referral evidence of 'a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system' against 'a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.' Raskin called the referral 'baseless' and predicted it would be 'laughed out of court.'

The specific perjury allegation turns on whether Smith's testimony that he sought only 'toll records,' not message contents, from lawmakers was knowingly false -- versus Raskin's competing account that the message contents Jordan cites came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, a different legal mechanism than a subpoena directed at lawmakers themselves

No DOJ charge, indictment, or formal investigation opening was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry -- the referral is a request, and Acting AG Blanche made no specific prosecutorial commitment

The roughly seven-month gap between the December 2025 deposition and the July 2026 referral, combined with the referral's timing well after the deposition's content was known, is presented here as a fact pattern without asserting a specific political motive beyond what Smith's counsel and Raskin have publicly alleged

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Whistleblower Protection Act / First Amendment Retaliation Against Federal Employees -- NOT charged criminally; challenged via a federal civil lawsuit and Office of Special Counsel complaints, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: On September 4, 2025, two former senior NIH officials -- Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID, the position Dr. Anthony Fauci previously held), and Dr. Kathleen Neuzil, former director of NIH's Fogarty International Center -- filed a joint whistleblower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel alleging they were forced out of their positions in retaliation for objecting to the cancellation of research grants and clinical trials, the politicization of scientific decisions, and what they described as baseless hostility toward vaccines from newly installed NIH leadership. Marrazzo, who had been placed on indefinite leave in March 2025, alleged Principal Deputy NIAID Director Dr. Matthew Memoli made statements mirroring Kennedy's views that 'vaccines are unnecessary if populations are healthy' and that NIH 'should not focus on vaccines.' Neuzil, placed on administrative leave April 12, 2025 before involuntarily resigning, separately objected to NIH canceling grants based on what she called 'anti-South Africa hostility' and an incorrect belief that certain grants advanced diversity, equity, and inclusion goals. Both officials' complaint also alleged that a $500 million universal-flu-vaccine program NIH awarded in May 2025 bypassed normal scientific peer review despite relying on technology multiple scientists described as badly outdated. Twenty-two days after filing the OSC complaint, on September 26, 2025, Secretary Kennedy fired Marrazzo outright. Marrazzo subsequently sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, naming Kennedy, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Memoli, and NIH as defendants, alleging the termination violated the Fifth Amendment's due process guarantee, the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, the Administrative Procedure Act, the First Amendment, and the Whistleblower Protection Act.

The employee's supervising official had knowledge of the protected activity
An adverse employment action (termination) followed the protected activity within a timeframe supporting an inference of retaliation
The stated agency rationale for the action does not independently account for the timing or the specific retaliatory statements alleged

official: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and former (2017-2021) senior White House adviser; private investor via his firm Affinity Partners
offense_category: Foreign Self-Dealing -- a president's family member profiting from a foreign government's favorable treatment of his private business while that same government simultaneously seeks better relations with the president's own administration; not itself a charged offense, but a documented conflict-of-interest and foreign-influence concern
incident_summary: Affinity Partners, the investment firm Jared Kushner founded after leaving his White House post, partnered with Dubai billionaire Mohamed Alabbar to develop a roughly $500 million Trump Tower hotel and apartment complex in Belgrade, Serbia, on the site of the former Yugoslav army headquarters -- a building bombed by NATO in 1999 and protected as a cultural monument. The Serbian government, led by President Aleksandar Vučić, agreed to grant Affinity Partners a 99-year lease to the site at no cost and, in November 2025, passed legislation to fast-track the project's approval; Vučić's government publicly framed the deal as a way to strengthen ties with the Trump administration at a time when the U.S. had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned NIS, Serbia's Russian-controlled oil monopoly. Removing the site's historic-monument protection required an expert opinion from Serbia's Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments; Serbian organized-crime prosecutors found that opinion had been forged, and on December 15, 2025 indicted Serbian Culture Minister Nikola Selaković -- a close Vučić ally -- along with three other officials on charges of abuse of office and document falsification for their roles in stripping that protection to clear the way for the project. Hours after the indictments were announced, Affinity Partners withdrew its application, stating it was 'stepping aside... out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade' -- withdrawing only once the underlying corruption became a criminal matter, not before, despite sustained public protests against the project throughout 2025.

The host government (Serbia) explicitly linked the project to improving relations with the Trump administration, at a time when the U.S. was applying economic pressure (tariffs, sanctions) on that same government

Serbian prosecutors found the specific legal step needed to enable the project -- removing the site's cultural-monument protection -- rested on a forged official document, leading to criminal indictments of the country's culture minister and three others
Kushner's firm withdrew only after the indictments were announced, not in response to the year-long public controversy and protests that preceded them

official: Kelly Loeffler, Administrator of the Small Business Administration
offense_category: Hatch Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §7323, prohibiting partisan political activity by federal employees using official resources) — NOT charged criminally, addressed via Office of Special Counsel complaint process; this entry has stronger documentary evidence (cited internal emails) than the parallel Turner/HUD entry in this dataset

A House committee letter to Loeffler cited these specific internal emails and characterized the conduct as 'a gross misuse of federal resources and a betrayal of public trust,' separately noting career civil servants do not swear their oath to a political party. Public Citizen also filed a Hatch Act complaint against Loeffler personally alleging she engaged in 'electioneering' while on duty during the same shutdown period.

official: Matthew Lohmeier, Under Secretary of the Air Force
offense_category: Confirmation of a Nominee With a Documented Pattern of Threatening Reprisal Against Named Military Officers and Spreading January 6 Disinformation -- confirmation itself is not unlawful, but the underlying record raises a civilian-military-boundary concern this tracker documents (a senior DoD civilian leader on record threatening 'serious consequences' against specific officers for perceived political disloyalty)
incident_summary: Matthew Lohmeier, a former Space Force lieutenant colonel relieved of command of the 11th Space Warning Squadron in 2021 after publicly alleging the military was embracing Marxism and 'critical race theory,' was nominated by Trump as Under Secretary of the Air Force -- the Air Force's second-highest-ranking civilian position. Sen. Jack Reed, at Lohmeier's May 2025 Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing, read aloud an October 19, 2024 social-media post in which Lohmeier warned of 'serious consequences' for senior military leaders who 'participated in the hyper-politicization of the uniformed services' if Trump won the election. Separately, Lohmeier had posted claims alleging 'undercover government agents' were present at the Capitol on January 6, 2021 -- while denying he used the word 'hoax,' he maintained government operatives had been present during the attack. Asked at his hearing whether he disavowed the October 2024 'serious consequences' post, Lohmeier deflected, saying he wanted to examine 'the context of all of the statements' and would hold accountable only those 'who don't follow the law and who don't honor their oath to the Constitution.' Sen. Mazie Hirono pressed him specifically on whether he would seek reprisal against named officers, including Lt. Gen. Stephen Whiting (who by that point led U.S. Space Command as a four-star general); Lohmeier did not directly answer, prompting Hirono to call his response 'totally not reassuring.' Despite Democratic opposition citing this record as disqualifying, the Senate confirmed Lohmeier 52-46 along party lines on July 24, 2025.

official: Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce
offense_category: Failure to honor a legally required 31-day health-insurance continuation period for terminated federal employees, and continued deduction of health-insurance premiums from paid-through employees without corresponding coverage or refund
incident_summary: Hundreds of Commerce Department employees -- including at NOAA and the CHIPS for America program -- fired as part of the administration's probationary-employee terminations were stripped of federal health insurance without notice, despite having paid their premiums and being legally entitled to a 31-day continuation-of-coverage grace period after termination. When a court order briefly required their reinstatement, some employees were restored to payroll only to be retroactively re-fired once an appeals court allowed the firings to proceed, with Commerce basing insurance-coverage cutoffs on employees' ORIGINAL termination dates rather than treating the reinstatement period as continuous coverage -- leaving a gap in which employees believed, and in some cases were told, they were insured. At least one NOAA employee, who had a long-planned hip arthroscopic surgery, now owes roughly $15,000 out of pocket after her coverage lapsed without her knowledge. Half a dozen former Commerce/NOAA/CHIPS employees reported that even their final pay stubs (for the pay period ending April 19, 2025) showed continued deductions for health-insurance premiums, despite their coverage having already lapsed. Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-MA), ranking member-adjacent on House Oversight, sent Secretary Lutnick a formal letter demanding an explanation for why the department did not honor the 31-day continuation requirement, why premiums continued to be deducted after coverage lapsed, and calling for full reimbursement of employees' out-of-pocket medical costs and premium overpayments.
elements_required: Federal employees are legally entitled to a 31-day health-insurance continuation period following termination -- a specific, checkable statutory/regulatory requirement, not a discretionary courtesy

Commerce Department employees were terminated, in some cases reinstated by court order and then re-terminated, with insurance coverage administered based on original (not reinstatement-adjusted) termination dates, producing coverage gaps
At least one specific, named-circumstance harm (the $15,000 surgery bill) is documented as a direct financial consequence
Premiums continued to be deducted from pay after coverage had already lapsed, for which no refund had been issued as of the formal congressional inquiry
A formal congressional oversight demand was made directly to the responsible Cabinet secretary, not just outside advocacy criticism

official: Linda McMahon, Secretary of Education
offense_category: Staffing a Federal Agency With Activists From Groups Whose Stated Goal Is Dismantling That Agency's Own Mission, Including the Secretary's Own Prior Leadership Role at One Such Group -- no criminal charge; an accountability claim about institutional capture and an undisclosed personal history rather than a specific statutory violation
incident_summary: Before becoming Education Secretary, McMahon chaired the America First Policy Institute (AFPI), a think tank co-founded by Stephen Miller that lists private-school vouchers and embedding 'biblical principles' in education among its priorities. ProPublica's investigation, published across a series of 2025-2026 reports, found McMahon has since brought at least 20 political appointees into the Education Department from ultraconservative advocacy groups and think tanks that share her department's own stated skepticism of public education's value, including at least nine from AFPI itself. Top adviser Lindsey Burke is a longtime Heritage Foundation policy director and the lead author of the education section of Project 2025, the conservative policy blueprint. Leaders from Moms for Liberty -- a group whose co-founder, Tiffany Justice (now with Heritage Foundation's political-advocacy arm), told ProPublica she hopes to drive public-school enrollment to 'zero' -- have joined McMahon for department roundtables and official events, and appointees with ties to Defending Education have also been placed in department posts. Under this leadership, the department has redirected hundreds of millions of dollars toward charter, private, and religious schools; released a formal 'Patriotic Education Supplemental Priority' tying federal funding preference to curricula emphasizing patriotic themes; and moved to protect school prayer. Separately, the department's Office for Civil Rights (OCR) had its staff cut roughly in half early in Trump's second term and its nationwide regional office footprint reduced; OCR resolved 30% fewer discrimination complaints in 2025 than in 2024 and reached formal resolution agreements in fewer than 1% of its investigations, while the administration's own subsequent budget proposal sought a further 35% cut to OCR's funding. In an apparent reversal reflecting the cuts' own dysfunction, the department later walked back hundreds of the OCR layoffs and paid approximately $38 million to the laid-off staff, even as OCR continued dismissing the large majority of complaints it received.

The department's civil-rights enforcement function (OCR) was cut roughly in half in staffing and saw a documented, quantified decline in complaint resolutions during the same period the department pursued the appointees' shared ideological agenda

incident_summary: On December 31, 2025, Trump vetoed H.R. 504, the Miccosukee Reserved Area Amendments Act, a bipartisan bill (sponsored by Rep. Carlos Gimenez) directing the Interior Department to work with the Miccosukee Tribe to protect homes, water systems, and wastewater infrastructure at the tribe's Osceola Camp inside Everglades National Park from repeated flooding. In his official veto message, published by the White House, Trump wrote that 'the Miccosukee Tribe has actively sought to obstruct reasonable immigration policies that the American people decisively voted for when I was elected' -- an explicit reference to the tribe's ongoing federal litigation opposing the administration's 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant detention facility, built in the Big Cypress National Preserve near tribal ceremonial sites and villages the tribe says the facility threatens. The veto message separately argued the federal government should not fund protections for 'an area that the Tribe has never been authorized to occupy' (Osceola Camp dates to 1935) and characterized the bill as 'special interests' funding 'unaligned with' the administration's immigration-enforcement policy. Tribal Chairman Talbert Cypress responded that the bill 'was not about special treatment, but about public safety, environmental stewardship, and honoring long-recognized tribal interests,' reflecting 'years of bipartisan work.' Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Trump's description of the tribe in the veto message was 'accurate.' The House attempted to override the veto on January 8, 2026, voting 236-188 in favor -- short of the 287 votes (two-thirds) required. This veto was issued the same day as a separate veto of H.R. 131, the Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act (a Colorado water-infrastructure bill), which is documented separately in doj-tina-peters-conviction-review-2025.json as part of a distinct retaliation pattern against Colorado over Tina Peters; the two vetoes share only a signing date, not a common grievance or target.

official: Chad Mizelle, former DOJ Chief of Staff and senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi
offense_category: Public Solicitation of Politically-Screened Hiring for Career (Nonpartisan) Federal Prosecutor Positions -- assistant U.S. attorneys are, by law and longstanding DOJ practice, career civil-service positions meant to be filled and evaluated apolitically, distinct from the political appointees at DOJ leadership
incident_summary: In early February 2026, Chad Mizelle -- former DOJ chief of staff and a senior adviser to Attorney General Pam Bondi -- publicly called for lawyers who 'support President Trump' to apply for career federal prosecutor positions, suggesting he could help such applicants secure the jobs. Assistant U.S. attorneys, who investigate and prosecute federal cases, are supposed to be nonpolitical and nonpartisan career civil servants, distinct from DOJ's political-appointee leadership. About forty minutes after Mizelle's post, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller amplified it, adding 'Patriots needed.' The call came amid mounting DOJ turmoil over politically charged personnel decisions, including the firing of prosecutors and investigators connected to earlier Trump-related cases and the pursuit of investigations against several of the President's political opponents. A former federal prosecutor quoted in ABC News's reporting warned that explicitly recruiting career prosecutors on the basis of political loyalty could be 'dangerous' to the office's traditional independence. That call was followed by a concrete policy change: MS NOW (Rachel Maddow Show) reported DOJ began waiving standard experience requirements for new federal prosecutor hires, allowing some candidates straight out of law school to be hired, amid widespread career-prosecutor departures and reported difficulty recruiting qualified replacements given the loyalty-test dynamic Mizelle's post captured.
elements_required: A senior former DOJ official with a continuing advisory role to the sitting Attorney General publicly solicited applicants for career (not political-appointee) federal prosecutor positions using explicit political-loyalty language ('support President Trump')
A senior White House official amplified the same call using similarly loyalty-coded language ('Patriots needed') within the same hour
Assistant U.S. attorney positions are, by design and longstanding DOJ norm, meant to be filled and evaluated on professional merit rather than political allegiance

The call occurred amid documented, separate instances of DOJ personnel actions against career staff connected to Trump-related investigations, providing context for concern that political-loyalty screening was already an operative practice, not merely rhetorical

evidence.description: ABC News's reporting confirms Mizelle's public call for Trump-supporting lawyers to apply for career federal prosecutor roles, that he suggested he could help such applicants get hired, and that Stephen Miller reposted the message roughly forty minutes later adding 'Patriots needed'; a former federal prosecutor is quoted warning the practice could be 'dangerous'
evidence.maps_to_element: Mizelle's solicitation and Miller's amplification, both using political-loyalty language

evidence.description: Newsweek's reporting confirms the call drew criticism from conservative legal commentators as well, not solely from Democratic-aligned sources, describing it as controversial across the political spectrum
evidence.maps_to_element: Breadth of concern about the loyalty-screening call, including from ideologically sympathetic commentators

evidence.description: MSNBC's coverage situates the Mizelle/Miller exchange within the context of AUSAs' traditional nonpartisan role, distinct from DOJ's political appointees, and frames it as departing from that norm
evidence.maps_to_element: AUSA positions' traditional nonpartisan role as the baseline the call departs from

evidence.description: The New York Times reported that DOJ has lost 21% of its attorneys (more than 2,600 lawyers) in 16 months and about 5,500 employees overall since the start of Trump's second term, and that support for the President has become an unusual and unprecedented prerequisite for career employees -- with the Times noting this dynamic appears to be contributing to the same staffing shortages Mizelle's recruitment call was intended to solve

official: Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Potential violation of 18 U.S.C. §592 (federal statute prohibiting the stationing of armed forces/law enforcement at polling places to influence an election) — NOT charged; as of this entry, no ICE deployment at polling places has actually occurred, so this documents a stated refusal to rule out conduct that would violate the statute, not a completed violation
incident_summary: During his March 2026 confirmation hearing and in subsequent public statements, Mullin repeatedly declined to rule out positioning ICE agents near or at polling places ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, stating he didn't understand the concern about immigration enforcement at voting sites. His comments were at odds with federal law expressly barring the stationing of law enforcement officers or military personnel at polling places. State election officials had asked Mullin, before his confirmation, to confirm in writing that ICE agents would not be sent to the polls; no indication has been found that he did so.
elements_required: 18 U.S.C. §592 prohibits any officer of the Army or Navy, or other person in the Armed Forces, from being present at any polls during an election in a manner that could constitute intimidation (the statute's precise scope as applied to civilian DHS/ICE personnel rather than military is a live legal question worth confirming with current case law)
Statement or action by the official indicating willingness to deploy enforcement personnel to polling locations
Absence of a clear, affirmative commitment not to do so despite direct requests
Actual deployment, if it occurs, would be the completed violation; statements alone establish intent/willingness, not yet a completed offense

evidence.description: During his March 2026 confirmation hearing, Mullin stated 'I don't understand what the concern about enforcing immigration at polling places is anyways... because, honestly, if you're not a citizen, you shouldn't be voting anyways,' declining to rule out ICE presence at polls
evidence.maps_to_element: Statement indicating willingness; absence of affirmative commitment not to deploy

evidence.description: Reporting confirms Mullin's comments were at odds with federal law expressly barring the stationing of law enforcement officers or members of the military at polling places, and also contradicted recent statements from senior DHS and ICE officials including a senior DHS election-integrity official who told state authorities ICE would not be dispatched to polling places
evidence.maps_to_element: Statutory framework; internal inconsistency with DHS's own other officials' representations

evidence.description: State election chiefs asked Mullin before his confirmation to confirm in writing that ICE agents would not be sent to the polls under his leadership; reporting found no indication he did so
evidence.maps_to_element: Absence of affirmative commitment despite direct request

evidence.description: Trump signed a March 31, 2026 executive order directing DHS, with the Social Security Administration, to compile and transmit state citizenship lists to election officials before federal elections; Mullin confirmed DHS was actively reviewing voter information ahead of the midterms under this order
evidence.maps_to_element: Context establishing DHS's active, expanding role in election-adjacent activity under Mullin

evidence.description: Trump's former chief strategist Steve Bannon suggested a separate ICE deployment to major U.S. airports during a DHS funding lapse was a 'test run' for using federal officers to interfere in the November elections, a characterization DHS did not appear to publicly rebut in the sourced reporting
evidence.maps_to_element: Context/pattern evidence, attributed to a third party (Bannon), not Mullin himself -- flag as a separate person's characterization

evidence.description: On CNN's 'State of the Union' on June 14, 2026 -- two weeks before this entry's own prior last_verified date -- Mullin narrowed his position for the first time, saying ICE would 'only' be deployed at polling places if a 'threat' arose, giving the example: 'if a threat were to arise, for whatever reason, at a polling station -- say a bomb threat would be called in -- our ICE agents are more than just immigration customs enforcement.' This statement predates this entry's original sourcing but was not incorporated when the entry was first written.
evidence.maps_to_element: First narrowing of Mullin's position from a flat refusal to rule out deployment to a conditional, threat-based carve-out

evidence.description: In a July 27, 2026 statement to Raw Story, DHS moved further, stating in writing: 'ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.' This is DHS's clearest statement to date that ICE does not intend to target polling places, but it preserves the same threat-based exception Mullin described in June, which voting-rights advocates have characterized as vague enough to function as a loophole for a pretextual 'threat.'
evidence.maps_to_element: DHS's most recent official position -- narrower non-deployment language than a flat refusal to commit, but still short of the unconditional written assurance state election officials originally requested

status: As of this update, DHS's position has evolved from Mullin's March 2026 flat refusal to rule out ICE presence at polls to a narrower, conditional formulation: Mullin said on June 14, 2026 that ICE would deploy 'only' in response to a 'threat' (e.g., a bomb threat), and DHS put a similar position in writing to Raw Story on July 27, 2026 -- 'ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations' but may make arrests at a polling location as the result of a 'targeted enforcement action' tied to an 'active public safety threat.' No completed deployment of ICE to a polling place has been identified as of this update, and no unconditional written non-deployment commitment of the kind state election officials originally requested has been given -- DHS's own language keeps a threat-based exception open. No new deployment has occurred; this remains a documented pattern of conditional, narrowing-but-incomplete assurances rather than either a completed violation or a clean resolution.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: Mullin's comments reflected general support for citizenship verification and election security, not a specific plan to station agents at polls; ICE has broad jurisdiction and a blanket promise to never be near any polling location anywhere would be operationally unrealistic; no deployment has actually occurred.
comeback: The distinction between 'general support for election security' and 'willingness to station immigration enforcement at polling places' collapses when a specific, simple written commitment was directly requested by state election officials and never given. State election administrators aren't asking for a policy philosophy -- they're asking for an operational assurance they can plan around, and the refusal to provide it is itself the documented concern. Worth keeping this entry framed carefully in debate as 'a documented refusal to provide the standard written assurance that federal law enforcement won't be used to chill voter participation' -- not as 'ICE went to the polls,' which would be inaccurate and easily rebutted.
cause: The Bannon characterization ('test run') is a third-party statement rather than established fact, and shouldn't be treated as sourced evidence about Mullin's intent. The more defensible framing: an administration that has used immigration enforcement in an expanding set of public venues (courthouses, churches, schools, airports during funding lapses) in ways courts have repeatedly found legally questionable, and that has declined to draw a bright line excluding polling places. Whether this reflects a deliberate incremental-expansion strategy or ad hoc enforcement overreach is genuinely uncertain, and should be presented that way in debate.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the documented statements themselves (Mullin's March and June comments, DHS's July 27 statement to Raw Story) -- directly sourced and uncontested. This recheck found that Mullin's June 14, 2026 'only if a threat arises' carve-out predates this entry's own original last_verified date (2026-06-30) by two weeks but was not incorporated when the entry was first written -- an omission-at-build-time, not a new development since. The DHS statement to Raw Story on July 27, 2026 is a genuinely new, post-last_verified development: DHS's clearest written non-deployment language yet, though it preserves the same threat-based exception rather than the unconditional commitment originally requested. LOW-MODERATE confidence remains on whether any of this constitutes an actual statutory violation, since no deployment has occurred. Best used in debate as 'DHS has repeatedly declined to give an unconditional non-deployment commitment, offering instead a narrowing series of threat-based carve-outs that critics say could be used pretextually' -- not as 'DHS deployed agents to polling places,' which has not happened.

official: Markwayne Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Misuse of a Federal Database / Unverified Public Claims Undermining Election Confidence -- DHS urged states to purge voter rolls using a system built for benefits-eligibility screening, not citizenship verification, after removing the system's own accuracy disclaimer, based on an unverified 250,000-noncitizen figure -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin urged state election officials to 'scrub' voter rolls using the expanded SAVE (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements) system, claiming 250,000 noncitizens are registered to vote across four states -- California, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Nevada -- without explaining how DHS verified that figure. SAVE was originally built to verify eligibility for government benefits, not to confirm citizenship for voter-registration purposes; the Trump administration expanded the system in 2025 to query voter registration data nationally using Social Security numbers and demographic information. A USCIS fact sheet that had acknowledged SAVE 'may not be able to confirm U.S. citizenship for individuals not designated as citizens in SSA records' was subsequently removed from public view. The Social Security Administration itself has said its citizenship data provides only 'a snapshot,' not 'definitive information about citizenship status,' and a 2006 federal audit found SSA had misclassified 3.3 million U.S. citizens as noncitizens, with 7% of people SSA flagged as noncitizens turning out to be eligible voters. Utah's own comprehensive SAVE-based review flagged 9,000 voters as potential noncitizens, but manual review found more than 5,600 of them were, in fact, U.S. citizens -- a majority-error rate. Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar called DHS's 250,000 figure 'wildly speculative at best,' and voting rights experts characterized the underlying data process as 'garbage in, garbage out.' Former Texas Secretary of State Jane Nelson separately warned about SAVE's accuracy based on county registrars' experience obtaining citizenship documentation that contradicted SAVE's flags. Update 2026-08-18: the same July 17, 2026 announcement in which Mullin made the 250,000-noncitizen claim and sent the four states' letters also included, at a same-day press conference, explicit threats that noncompliant election officials could face 'fines, ... penalties, and even, depending on how far it goes, prison time,' and that noncompliant states could lose federal election-security grant funding -- a materially more coercive characterization than 'urged,' corroborated across ABC News, Common Dreams, and States Newsroom/Herald and News coverage of the same speech and letters.
elements_required: DHS publicly claimed a specific noncitizen-voter-registration figure without explaining its verification methodology
The system used (SAVE) was designed and built for a different purpose (benefits eligibility) than the one it is now being used for (citizenship/voter-roll verification)
DHS or USCIS removed its own prior public disclaimer about the system's reliability limitations for this use case
Independent, real-world application of the same system (Utah's review) produced a documented, high error rate flagging actual citizens as noncitizens

official: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
offense_category: Evasion of Court-Ordered Testimony Regarding DOGE's Dismantlement of Federal Agencies -- a civil-litigation accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: Beginning in mid-November 2025, constables and private process servers made repeated attempts -- including at least four separate attempts at Musk's Brownsville, Texas property near SpaceX headquarters, and at his West Lake Hills, Texas residence -- to serve Musk with a subpoena for deposition testimony regarding his role in DOGE's dismantlement of federal agencies, including USAID. Process servers were repeatedly denied entry to gated properties, and staff told servers Musk was not home and no one was authorized to accept paperwork on his behalf. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang ruled in early February 2026 that Musk and State Department officials must sit for depositions regarding USAID's dismantlement, rejecting a motion for a protective order that argued the testimony was barred by protections for high-ranking officials. The Justice Department intervened on Musk's behalf in the litigation. offense_category: Statutory Violation -- proceeding with major White House construction without congressional authorization, addressed here as a rule-of-law/separation-of-powers question rather than a criminal charge; a federal district court found the White House's own $2.5 million annual maintenance-and-repair appropriation does not authorize demolition and new construction of this scale
incident_summary: President Trump ordered the 123-year-old East Wing and the Jacqueline Kennedy Garden demolished to build a roughly 90,000-square-foot ballroom, with its publicly announced cost escalating from an initial $200 million estimate to $300 million and then $400 million, funded by private donors including Amazon, Apple, Google, and other corporations with business before the federal government (a White House official said $350 million had been raised as of October 2025). On December 12, 2025, the National Trust for Historic Preservation -- the organization Congress itself designated to help protect historic federal sites -- filed suit in U.S. District Court for D.C., represented by former Clinton/Obama White House counsel Greg Craig, seeking to halt construction until the standard federal review and public-comment process was completed, arguing 'no president is legally allowed to tear down portions of the White House without any review whatsoever ... [or] construct a ballroom on public property without giving the public the opportunity to weigh in.' On March 31, 2026, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ordered construction to stop, ruling that no statute 'comes close' to giving the president unilateral authority to proceed without congressional authorization; Leon specifically found that 40 U.S.C. section 7305's roughly $2.5 million congressionally appropriated White House maintenance-and-repair fund covers 'things like replacing the lightbulbs, fixing broken furniture and changing the wallpaper, not wholesale demolition of entire buildings and construction of new ones.' The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed Leon's preliminary injunction in August 2026, holding Congress has 'exclusive constitutional authority over federal property like the White House.' The Supreme Court, in a 5-4 order on August 31, 2026, stayed the injunction and allowed construction to resume while the underlying case continues, on the ground that the National Trust likely lacks legal standing to sue -- a procedural ruling, not a merits finding that the project is lawful. Chief Justice Roberts wrote the dissent, joined by Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson, arguing the ballroom construction 'is likely unlawful' and that the project likely requires congressional authorization -- meaning the Chief Justice himself agreed with the district court and D.C. Circuit's merits conclusion even while being outvoted on the separate standing question that actually decided the stay. Separately, Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced legislation in December 2025 to remove the White House's existing statutory exemption from National Historic Preservation Act Section 106 review and require public input on future White House renovations -- itself confirming that exemption currently exists and that the litigation's live legal theory rests on the National Capital Planning Act's construction-authorization framework, not Section 106 (from which the White House complex is statutorily exempt).
elements_required: The White House's own annual congressionally-appropriated maintenance-and-repair fund (40 U.S.C. section 7305, roughly $2.5 million) is limited by its own terms to ordinary maintenance and repair, not demolition and new construction of this scale -- a federal district judge's own textual finding, not merely an advocacy characterization

offense_category: Misuse of Administrative Subpoena Power to Target Protected Speech -- no criminal charge; this is a First Amendment/investigative-power-abuse accountability claim, distinguished from a judicial subpoena because administrative subpoenas require no judge's approval
incident_summary: A Washington Post investigation found DHS used administrative subpoenas -- which, unlike grand jury or judicial subpoenas, require no judge's sign-off -- to obtain personal data on government critics and people engaged in constitutionally protected speech, including at least one case in which DHS sought to identify a person who had emailed a DHS attorney criticizing the agency's handling of an asylum seeker's case. Following the Post's reporting, a bipartisan group of three Democratic and three Republican lawmakers, led by Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Adriano Espaillat, introduced the Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act, which would require government officials to certify under penalty of perjury that they are not using subpoenas to monitor or retaliate against people exercising free-speech or other constitutionally protected activity, and would separately limit the government's ability to obtain phone records without a judge's order. Harvard sued DHS the next day, May 23, 2025, alleging the revocation violated the First Amendment (retaliation for protected activity), the Administrative Procedure Act, and due process; U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs granted a temporary restraining order that same day, then a preliminary injunction on June 20, 2025, finding Harvard was likely to succeed on the merits. DHS did not relent: on July 9, 2025, it escalated with administrative subpoenas demanding Harvard turn over records, communications, and other documents on immigration-law-enforcement compliance dating back to January 1, 2020, publicly accusing the university of enabling visa abuse and 'advocating violence.' On August 2, 2025, Harvard agreed to comply with a related DHS subpoena for employment verification forms covering thousands of staff, while withholding some student job records over privacy concerns, as the administration simultaneously pressed Harvard with a separate $2.6 billion research-funding freeze (see government-services/entries/harvard-research-funding-freeze-2025.json). On August 7, 2025, DHS stipulated it would not use the original May 22 letter as a basis to revoke Harvard's SEVP certification -- a concession that stopped short of formally abandoning the underlying legal position. The injunction blocking the revocation has remained in effect through 2026, upheld by the First Circuit, with the underlying case still unresolved.

offense_category: Suppressing an Inspector General Finding to Evade a Statutory Deadline, Then Giving Congress a Contradicted Sworn Account of Compliance
incident_summary: In July 2025, DHS ended the requirement in place since 2006 that airline passengers remove their shoes during TSA security screening. A classified DHS Inspector General report completed in November 2025, based on undercover 'red team' testing, found that many of the full-body scanners used at TSA checkpoints cannot effectively detect threats concealed in shoes -- meaning the policy change created a documented new security vulnerability. The Inspector General's office alerted Secretary Noem's office to the finding in August 2025. Rather than taking public or substantive corrective action, Noem's DHS reclassified the report, elevating it and limiting its release, despite a statutory requirement that the department address the issue by January 30, 2026. In subsequent sworn testimony to lawmakers, Noem stated that 'all of the recommendations' in the Inspector General's report had already been implemented. A March 4, 2026 memo from Inspector General Joseph Cuffari's office stated it had not received any evidence supporting that claim. Sen. Tammy Duckworth formally demanded DHS rescind the 'shoes on' policy, citing the watchdog's finding that it 'created a new security vulnerability.'

official: Donald Trump, President (acting on activist Laura Loomer's recommendation)
offense_category: Firing the Nation's Top Signals-Intelligence and Military Cyber Officials Based on an Outside Activist's Personal Loyalty Test, Leaving the NSA and Cyber Command Without Senate-Confirmed Leadership for Nearly a Year
incident_summary: On April 3-4, 2025, President Trump fired Gen. Timothy Haugh, the Senate-confirmed director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command, along with his civilian deputy Wendy Noble -- roughly a year into what is traditionally a three-year term, and with no public explanation of an official reason. Multiple outlets (ABC News, The Daily Beast, Breaking Defense) reported the firings followed a private Oval Office meeting in which far-right activist Laura Loomer presented Trump a list of roughly a dozen officials she deemed insufficiently loyal, and specifically urged Haugh's and Noble's removal; Loomer publicly took credit afterward, stating Haugh was fired for being 'disloyal' and noting he had been appointed under Gen. Mark Milley, whom Trump has accused of treason. Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that Loomer 'had nothing to do with' the firings -- directly contradicting Loomer's own public account. Lt. Gen. William Hartman (Haugh's own deputy) and Sheila Thomas assumed acting leadership of Cyber Command and the NSA, respectively. The agency then went without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director for nearly a year: by November 2025, Defense One, Nextgov/FCW, and Government Executive reported a 'leadership vacuum' had produced sustained morale problems ('the morale inside the organization is rather depressed... that's what happens when your boss disappears'), a wave of additional senior departures -- including NSA's top lawyer, April Falcon Doss, reportedly also let go on Loomer's advice -- and a halt to recruitment for the NSA's Legal Honors Program, a key pipeline for the agency's legal talent. The White House had reportedly considered elevating Hartman to the permanent post but backed off those plans. In August 2025, NSA Director Tulsi Gabbard designated Joe Francescon -- an NSC veteran of Trump's first term -- as the agency's next deputy director, with Trump's approval; Loomer again intervened, publicizing a 2023 FEC record showing Francescon had donated $500 to Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, and the White House withdrew Francescon's nomination in December 2025 without another official reason given, extending the same vacancy pattern for a second time. Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) publicly criticized the White House's 'gross negligence' in letting Loomer drive the hiring process. Trump then nominated Army Lt. Gen. Joshua Rudd, then deputy commander of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, in December 2025; the Senate confirmed Rudd 71-29 on March 10, 2026, promoting him to four-star general, ending the vacancy. Some senators raised concerns during confirmation about Rudd's comparatively limited cyber-operations and signals-intelligence background relative to prior NSA/Cyber Command leaders.

Jamie Raskin sent a formal letter to FBI Director Kash Patel on June 18, 2025 demanding an investigation into the FBI's role in what he characterized as the unlawful detention of a sitting member of Congress.

offense_category: Waiving Standard Security-Clearance Polygraph Requirements for the FBI's Deputy Director and Two Personal Aides, Granting Top-Secret/SCI Access Despite Unresolved or Inconclusive Results
incident_summary: ProPublica reported on November 24, 2025 that FBI Director Kash Patel granted unprecedented polygraph waivers to three of his closest aides -- Deputy Director Dan Bongino, congressional-affairs liaison Marshall Yates, and Patel's personal assistant Nicole Rucker -- allowing all three to obtain Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) clearances, the level required for access to the nation's most sensitive intelligence, including presidential briefings, despite polygraph results that did not clear under normal standards. Sources told ProPublica that Yates and Rucker did not clear their polygraph exams; Bongino's specific results were not established in reporting. Former FBI officials said they could not recall any senior official ever receiving such a waiver, with one recalling only a single such waiver in seven years, granted to an outside subject-matter expert -- not a sitting senior FBI leader. The FBI's own employment guidelines require all employees to pass a polygraph as part of obtaining Top Secret clearance. An FBI Security Division employee filed a formal internal complaint with the division's director, Robert Turner, alleging the waivers violated agency policy, and separately shared the complaint with the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General. An FBI spokesperson denied that any of the three had 'failed' their polygraphs -- a characterization that leaves open whether the results were instead deemed inconclusive -- but declined to specify what, if anything, in ProPublica's reporting the FBI considered false.

FBI leadership maintains standards remain intact and that the change removes only duplicative steps for already-vetted internal employees. Critics, including retired supervisory special agent Jeff Crocker, argue the removed steps are key screening safeguards -- in-person interviews, Crocker told Reuters, are essential for evaluating a candidate's maturity, verbal communication, and analytical problem-solving skills that a written exam alone cannot assess.

offense_category: Inflating a Minor Protest Incident Into a Felony Prosecution That Failed at Every Stage -- a grand jury's refusal to indict and a subsequent jury acquittal are themselves strong evidence the felony theory lacked merit
incident_summary: In August 2025, Sean Dunn, a former DOJ paralegal, threw a Subway sandwich at a Customs and Border Patrol officer participating in Trump's federal law-enforcement surge in Washington, D.C. -- an incident he characterized as a protest. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office sought a felony assault charge carrying up to eight years in prison. A D.C. grand jury refused to indict Dunn on the felony charge, a step described in reporting as a notable rebuke joining a string of failed prosecutions against protesters arrested by the administration's militarized federal deployment. Rather than dropping the matter, Pirro's office then filed a misdemeanor assault charge against Dunn, which proceeded to trial. On November 6, 2025, a federal jury in Washington, D.C. found Dunn not guilty after only several hours of deliberation. Rather than accepting that outcome, the U.S. Attorney's office pursued a misdemeanor charge instead of declining to prosecute, which also failed at trial by jury acquittal

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Suspending Two Career Prosecutors Within Hours for Accurately Describing January 6 as a 'Mob of Rioters' in a Court Filing, Then Substituting a Sanitized Filing That Omitted the Defendant's Jan. 6 Involvement
incident_summary: On October 28, 2025, two career DOJ prosecutors, Carlos Valdivia and Samuel White, filed a sentencing memorandum in the case of Taylor Franklin Taranto -- a former January 6 defendant who received clemency from President Trump and was later separately convicted of weapons and hoax charges after being arrested near the Obamas' home in 2023 with firearms and ammunition in his van -- describing the events of January 6, 2021 factually: 'thousands of people comprising a mob of rioters attacked the U.S. Capitol while a joint session of Congress met to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election.' Within hours of the filing, both Valdivia and White were placed on administrative leave and locked out of their DOJ accounts. The next morning, the filing was replaced with a nearly identical 12-page memo, this time signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Travis Wolf on behalf of Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia -- the substitute version omitted any reference to Taranto's involvement in the January 6 riot itself, describing only his separate 2023 crimes near the Obama residence. At Taranto's sentencing hearing that Thursday, he received time served and three months of supervised release.

The altered filing's timing and content directly preceded and plausibly influenced a lenient sentencing outcome (time served) in a case involving weapons found near a former president's home

official: Donald Trump, President (signed the memorandum)
offense_category: Executive Reversal of a Longstanding Prohibition on Private-Sector Offensive Cyberoperations, Adopted Without New Legislation and Criticized as Under-Developed by Named Cybersecurity Experts
status: In effect -- NSPM signed Aug. 12, 2026; detailed implementing guidance due within two months; no participating companies publicly identified as of this writing
incident_summary: The New York Times reported in January 2026 that draft versions of the administration's forthcoming National Cybersecurity Strategy discussed expanding private companies' role in offensive cyberoperations, including 'hack back' authorities or mechanisms resembling historical Letters of Marque, drawing early concern from former military and intelligence officials. The administration's National Cybersecurity Strategy, released March 6, 2026 (a brief, three-to-five-page document), included language that the government would 'unleash the private sector by creating incentives to identify and disrupt adversary networks and scale our national capabilities,' though it stopped short of explicitly authorizing private cyberattacks at that stage. On August 12, 2026, Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM) that went further, directing a Homeland Security Task Force National Coordination Center to vet and authorize 'Participating Companies' to conduct offensive cyber surveillance (including spyware deployment) and disruptive attacks aimed at destroying data or systems belonging to foreign transnational criminal organizations, under federal direction and control. This reverses decades of U.S. policy that had prohibited private companies from conducting 'hack back' operations, which previously exposed firms to liability under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act regardless of the target's own conduct. The NSPM includes some oversight mechanisms: a two-month deadline for detailed implementing guidance, a $1 million escrow deposit from participating companies (forfeitable for non-compliance), a requirement that both the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security sign off on operations before execution, procedures intended to prevent targeting of Americans or U.S.-based systems, and a mandatory notification requirement if a participating company discovers an imminent attack on critical infrastructure. Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy, a cybersecurity firm, publicly called the policy 'half-baked,' warning that American personnel conducting these operations 'could easily be classified as non-uniformed combatants while traveling overseas,' exposing them to foreign prosecution -- a legal-exposure risk the memorandum itself does not appear to resolve. As of this writing, no specific companies have been publicly confirmed as enrolled participants; the White House did not respond to questions about whether any firms were already active under the program.
elements_required: A longstanding, decades-old U.S. policy prohibited private companies from conducting offensive 'hack back' cyberoperations
The President signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum reversing that prohibition via executive action, not new legislation
The memorandum's own stated oversight mechanisms (DOJ/DHS sign-off, escrow deposit, guidance deadline) were publicly documented alongside the authorization itself

A named cybersecurity-industry expert publicly characterized the policy's legal and operational safeguards as inadequate ('half-baked'), specifically flagging combatant-status/foreign-prosecution exposure risk for American personnel
No specific participating company had been publicly confirmed as of this writing, meaning the program's real-world operation and oversight in practice remains untested

Reversing a decades-old prohibition via executive memorandum, without new legislation clarifying personnel liability or international-law status, shifts a significant policy question away from congressional deliberation and toward implementing guidance the administration itself has two months to write -- guidance not yet public as of this writing.

official: William (Bill) Pulte, Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency; Acting Director of National Intelligence (dual role, beginning June 2026)
offense_category: Potential Misuse of Federal Authority/Confidential Financial Data (relevant standards: 12 U.S.C. provisions governing FHFA's regulatory data access; potential 18 U.S.C. §1905, unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by a government employee; potential Privacy Act of 1974 violation); separately, potential unlawful disclosure of grand jury material (Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(e)) — NOT charged; GAO investigation formally opened and underway, federal grand jury reportedly investigating a related matter, no findings or charges confirmed
incident_summary: Beginning April 2025, as FHFA director, Pulte made a series of criminal referrals to DOJ against prominent Trump critics and political opponents -- including NY AG Letitia James, Sen. Adam Schiff, Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, and Rep. Eric Swalwell -- alleging mortgage fraud, using mortgage data accessible through his oversight of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. DOJ opened a formal grand jury investigation into James on August 8, 2025 following Pulte's referral, subpoenaing records tied to her civil fraud judgment against Trump and her NRA lawsuit, and assigned Weaponization Working Group director Ed Martin to oversee the James and Schiff probes; Martin urged James to resign 'as an act of good faith' and, a week later, traveled to her Brooklyn home to pose for photos outside it, conduct her attorney called a violation of DOJ ethics rules. The referrals themselves bypassed FHFA's own inspector-general review process, with Pulte sending the accusations directly to Trump-aligned DOJ prosecutors instead -- a former DOJ inspector general called the approach 'highly irregular.' Public records showed Pulte paid fees to obtain Lisa Cook's mortgage documents in August 2025, the day before making a criminal referral against her. Fannie Mae officials who internally investigated whether Pulte improperly obtained Democratic officials' mortgage records were themselves removed: chief ethics officer Suzanne Libby was removed, general counsel Danielle McCoy resigned under pressure, and FHFA's acting inspector general Joe Allen, who had forwarded the internal findings to prosecutors, was asked to step down. On November 17, 2025, eight Senate Democrats led by Elizabeth Warren formally requested a GAO investigation; GAO confirmed on December 4, 2025 that it had accepted the request and opened a formal investigation into whether Pulte and FHFA employees misused federal authority and resources. Separately, Rep. Eric Swalwell filed a civil lawsuit against Pulte on November 25, 2025, alleging Pulte violated the Privacy Act of 1974 by accessing his mortgage records for political purposes. A federal grand jury in Maryland has also reportedly investigated whether Pulte and DOJ official Ed Martin illegally shared grand jury material with unauthorized parties in connection with the Schiff referral. After Reuters's inquiries, Bloomfield Township's director of assessing said the township would revoke the exemption on the Pultes' Michigan residence. Separately, on September 11, 2025, House Financial Services Committee ranking member Rep. Maxine Waters led House Democrats in a letter asking FHFA's own inspector general (distinct from the GAO investigation documented above) to review whether Pulte complied with applicable federal and agency rules in obtaining, reviewing, and publicly releasing Cook's mortgage records; in a CNBC interview around the same time, Pulte acknowledged he had received a 'tip' prompting the referral but declined to disclose its source.

incident_summary: Mark Zarkin, a Michigan restaurateur (owner of Steven Lelli's On The Green in Farmington Hills) and prominent Detroit-area Trump fundraiser with no documented housing-finance experience, was appointed by FHFA Director Bill Pulte as a consultant to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac after Pulte took office in March 2025. Six sources confirmed the role to Reuters, and Reuters found Zarkin still held an active Freddie Mac email account identifying him as a 'consultant' as recently as the weeks before publication. In 1999, Zarkin pleaded no contest to attempted third-degree sexual conduct in Macomb County, Michigan, after investigators recovered his DNA during a pelvic examination of a woman who was underage and 'mentally incapacitated' by alcohol and Valium; he was sentenced to eight months in jail, three years' probation, and mandatory sex-offender registration. In 2009, a judge granted his attorney's petition to vacate that conviction, reasoning Zarkin had not understood the registry requirement when he accepted the plea -- even though court records show registration was explicitly part of the original plea agreement, and the judge's order gave no further explanation; legal experts told Reuters the vacatur was 'unusual.' Separately, an ongoing 2025 Wayne County, Michigan lawsuit alleges Zarkin discussed with Jamiel Altaheri, the recently resigned Hamtramck police chief, a scheme to pay Trump as much as $5 million for a pardon of an unnamed New York associate accused of financial crimes; two plaintiffs, a former city manager and a former police officer, allege they lost their jobs partly for disclosing the plan. Zarkin denied everything by text message to Reuters, stating 'I have never been employed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. I also have no criminal record. Anything you say to the contrary is defamatory.' Pulte called Reuters' questions 'filled with completely false and defamatory statements' without elaborating, and FHFA's media office issued an unsigned statement calling 'nearly all' of Reuters' statements 'false, misleading, or defamatory,' also without specifics; Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

offense_category: Potential Politicization of Intelligence Analysis (violates longstanding Intelligence Community tradecraft standards requiring analysis be independent of policy preference, codified in Intelligence Community Directive 203; NOT a criminal statute violation, this is an institutional-integrity and professional-standards matter, addressed through oversight and public accountability, not prosecution)

official: John Ratcliffe, CIA Director; Tulsi Gabbard, Director of National Intelligence (attempted to fire officers assigned to DEIA programs without the appeal/reassignment process their own agencies' regulations require)
offense_category: Fifth Amendment due-process violation and agency-regulation noncompliance -- terminating federal officers without the internal appeal and reassignment process their own employment regulations require (a procedural/administrative-law claim, not itself an allegation that DEIA work was unlawful)
status: Blocked by courts -- the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed (2-1, July 2, 2026) a preliminary injunction requiring CIA and ODNI to give the 19 plaintiff-officers an internal appeal/reassignment process before any termination; the officers remain on paid administrative leave pending that process, and no final termination has taken effect as of this entry's last verification
incident_summary: Following Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order rolling back federal DEIA programs, CIA Director John Ratcliffe moved to terminate 51 career CIA officers who were on temporary rotational assignments to diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) programs, and ODNI under Director Tulsi Gabbard took parallel action against DEIA-assigned officers there. Ratcliffe publicly defended the move as building a 'colorblind meritocracy' focused solely on merit-based hiring and promotion; the New York Times reported May 13, 2025 that this was the first public clash between career intelligence officers and Trump's new spy-agency leadership over the DEIA rollback. Seventeen CIA officers and two ODNI officers (19 total) sued in February 2025, arguing the terminations violated their due-process rights and the agencies' own employment regulations, since the DEIA rotational assignments did not strip the officers of their permanent career positions or the reduction-in-force protections (appeal rights, consideration for other jobs) those positions carry. In late March 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga (E.D. Va., a George W. Bush appointee) issued a preliminary injunction barring the government from implementing the terminations, finding what Ratcliffe attempted functioned as a reduction in force triggering the officers' regulatory appeal and reassignment rights, and ordered the plaintiffs kept on paid administrative leave pending further proceedings. The government appealed. On July 2, 2026, a divided panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed Trenga's injunction 2-1; writing for the majority, Judge Nicole Berner held that CIA and ODNI had to honor the officers' Fifth Amendment due-process protections and follow their own existing regulations -- providing an internal appeal process and an opportunity for reassignment -- before terminating them, regardless of the CIA Director's broader statutory hiring/firing authority. Judge Paul Niemeyer dissented, arguing the ruling improperly constrained that authority. The panel's opinion also included pointed criticism of the government's legal arguments on appeal as beside the point.
elements_required: The affected officers held permanent career positions carrying Fifth Amendment due-process protections and/or agency reduction-in-force regulations (appeal rights, reassignment consideration), distinct from their temporary DEIA rotational assignments
The agencies attempted to terminate them without affording the internal appeal and reassignment process those protections/regulations require
A court (not just the plaintiffs) found the process afforded was legally deficient

rebuttal_anticipated: Ratcliffe and DOJ argued the CIA Director holds broad, largely unreviewable statutory authority under the National Security Act to hire and fire agency personnel in the interest of national security, and that the DEIA rotational assignments were themselves temporary details rather than the officers' permanent positions, so the ordinary RIF appeal/reassignment regulations should not have applied to ending those specific assignments.

Judge Niemeyer's dissent shows the question remains genuinely contested at the appellate level, and the government retains the option of seeking further review (en banc or Supreme Court), so this is a preliminary-injunction-stage win for the officers, not a final merits judgment.

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services (acting through his personal attorney and outside adviser Aaron Siri)
offense_category: Granting a Private Attorney With Direct Financial Stakes in Anti-Vaccine Litigation an Outsized, Non-Public Role in Vetting HHS Appointees and Shaping Department Policy
incident_summary: The New York Times reported October 3, 2025 that Aaron Siri -- Kennedy's personal attorney during his presidential campaign and a longtime legal ally in anti-vaccine litigation -- has held an unusually direct, non-public role inside Kennedy's HHS: helping vet candidates for departmental jobs and for membership on CDC's influential vaccine advisory committee (ACIP), while simultaneously filing lawsuits and FDA petitions on subjects squarely within HHS's own policy purview. Fired CDC Director Susan Monarez told senators in August 2025 that Kennedy had instructed her to meet with Siri, though she ultimately did not do so. Siri's law firm has pursued a specific-interest advocacy through vaccine-exemption litigation (partnering with West Virginia's governor in June 2024 on a religious-exemption lawsuit against the state's Board of Education, followed by HHS itself issuing reminders to states in September 2024 to respect religious exemptions), a December 2024 FDA petition to withdraw or suspend the standalone polio vaccine, multiple lawsuits against children's toothpaste makers over fluoride content, and a 12-page FDA petition demanding strengthened pregnancy warnings on Tylenol's label -- filed roughly two weeks before President Trump's September 22, 2025 address linking Tylenol use in pregnancy to autism, with Siri's firm having separately encouraged clients as early as 2023 to file Tylenol-autism litigation while related cases were pending. Siri's nonprofit client, the Informed Consent Action Network (run by Del Bigtree, Kennedy's former campaign communications director), has funneled substantial funding to Siri's firm -- $6 million in 2023 alone and roughly $13 million total since 2018 -- meaning Siri has a direct financial stake in the same anti-vaccine legal and policy landscape he has helped shape from inside the department vetting process. Legal-ethics expert Elizabeth Chamblee Burch said the arrangement raises 'insider influence' concerns about whether HHS decisions are 'backed by hard science and research' or shaped by Siri's outside interests. Diana Zuckerman, president of the National Center for Health Research, said she was interviewed by a senior partner at Siri's firm about a vaccine-committee position and asked whether she would be comfortable advocating that vaccine decisions be left 'entirely between parents and doctors' -- a position she read as anti-mandate advocacy -- and declined after concluding the interview was itself a form of ideological screening.

The same attorney's firm filed multiple lawsuits and FDA petitions on subjects (vaccine exemptions, fluoride, Tylenol/acetaminophen) directly within HHS's own policy authority during the same period
The Secretary personally directed at least one senior HHS/CDC official to meet with the attorney
Named legal-ethics experts characterized the arrangement as raising a genuine insider-influence conflict-of-interest concern, not merely political controversy
