official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Administrative Procedure Act Violation — Arbitrary and Capricious Agency Action (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A)) — judicial finding actually obtained against the agency's vaccine-advisory decisions; this is civil administrative law, not a criminal matter; separately, the CDC director's firing raises whistleblower-retaliation-adjacent concerns not yet tested in litigation
incident_summary:
Added 2026-09-09 (backfilling a dropped fold from commit ec8078a, which marked these records folded in candidates.json but never wrote the content here): antecedent mechanics of the June 2025 ACIP purge, months before the March 2026 litigation this entry primarily documents. Kennedy fired all 17 sitting ACIP members on June 9, 2025 (NYT), replacing them with eight new appointees, several with anti-vaccine ties; one appointee withdrew before the panel's first meeting, leaving seven members ahead of a vote on thimerosal (NYT, June 24, 2025). Ousted members and outside groups warned the shake-up, combined with concurrent CDC staff cuts, would weaken US immunization infrastructure (Reuters, June 16, 2025); insurers largely stayed silent on whether they would keep covering vaccines the new panel might drop, with only one major insurer committing to continued coverage as of early July 2025 (Wired, July 2025). Kennedy went on to appoint Vicky Pebsworth -- a nurse who has long claimed, contrary to scientific consensus, that vaccines caused her son's autism -- to the panel (Guardian, July 5, 2025), and the CDC separately hired Lyn Redwood, former head of Kennedy's own Children's Health Defense organization, to advise its vaccine safety office and present to the reconstituted ACIP (CBS News, June 2025). On July 23, 2025, HHS ended US distribution of thimerosal-containing flu vaccines, citing decades-old, scientifically unsupported claims linking the preservative to autism despite FDA assurances to the contrary (Reuters). In August 2025 the CDC expelled major medical associations, including the AMA and American Academy of Pediatrics, from vaccine-policy workgroups (AP, Aug 2025), and the panel's own ousted former members publicly condemned the purge in a New England Journal of Medicine article warning it abandoned scientific rigor and risked outbreaks (The Hill, Aug 2025).

Added 2026-09-09 (same backfill): the September 2025 Monarez-ouster crisis, referenced elsewhere in this entry only briefly, unfolded as follows. CDC Director Susan Monarez -- Senate-confirmed only weeks earlier -- was removed around August 27, 2025 after refusing to pre-approve ACIP vaccine recommendations without independent review and refusing to fire additional senior staff; she said she never resigned (Guardian, Aug 27, 2025), and by early September was telling reporters and, later, Congress (testimony the week of Sept 17, 2025) that she had been directly pressured to rubber-stamp the panel's recommendations (Reuters, Sept 4, 2025; NPR, Sept 17, 2025). At least three to four senior CDC leaders resigned in protest, some escorted out by security (NYT, Aug 28, 2025), amid broader turmoil Reuters described as roughly 2,400 CDC staff purged under Kennedy's tenure alongside a rollback of COVID-19 vaccine guidance for children and pregnant women (Reuters, Aug 28, 2025); by mid-September, four top officials and thousands of staff had exited and Kennedy had proposed a 42% CDC budget cut (Guardian, Sept 15, 2025). Former Principal Deputy Director Anne Schuchat warned the loss of experienced leadership left the country 'really at risk' (NPR, Aug 29, 2025). Nine former CDC directors from both parties, in a New York Times op-ed, said Kennedy's actions were 'endangering every American's health' (op-ed reported by CBS News, Sept 2025), and more than 20 medical organizations together with over 1,000 current and former HHS employees separately called for his resignation (Reuters, Sept 4, 2025). Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former head of NIH's infectious disease institute, filed a whistleblower complaint alleging retaliation for resisting Kennedy-directed cancellation of vaccine research (CBS News, Sept 2025). Even former Trump Surgeon General Jerome Adams called for Kennedy's firing (CNN, Sept 6, 2025). At Senate hearings the following week, Sen. Maria Cantwell and lawmakers in both parties called Kennedy a 'charlatan' over mRNA research cuts and the ACIP purge (NPR, Sept 5, 2025; Guardian, Sept 4, 2025), and Sen. Bill Cassidy -- whose vote had been decisive in confirming Kennedy -- separately warned the public not to trust the reshaped panel's coming changes to the childhood vaccine schedule (Reuters, Sept 17, 2025). Acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill, installed after Monarez's ouster, told staff the agency needed to end 'mission creep' and practice 'radical transparency' -- language Kennedy had also used days earlier in his own Wall Street Journal op-ed arguing the CDC should be limited to infectious-disease work (NBC News, Sept 2025; ABC News, Sept 2025). Separately, federal government lawyers themselves objected, on grounds it violated federal law, when Kennedy gave MIT professor and vaccine critic Retsef Levi sweeping authority -- setting agendas, appointing members, shaping recommendations -- over a CDC COVID-vaccine workgroup (Reuters, Sept 17, 2025). In a parallel purge at the FDA, vaccine expert and Kennedy critic Paul Offit was abruptly removed from the FDA's Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC) despite having already been cleared for another term through 2027 (Guardian, Sept 2, 2025). Monarez and former CDC Chief Medical Officer Debra Houry both testified to Congress the week of Sept 17, 2025 that they had been pressured to pre-approve panel recommendations without review, amid what was then the worst measles outbreak in 30 years (NPR and Guardian, Sept 2025); Houry separately described Kennedy's approach as a 'hostile takeover' of the agency (Guardian, Oct 4, 2025).

Added 2026-09-09 (same backfill): the reconstituted panel's own votes, later nullified in bulk by the March 16, 2026 ruling (see the stay's documented scope below), began in September 2025 -- on September 18, 2025 the panel voted 8-3 to drop the recommendation that children under four receive the combined MMRV vaccine rather than separate shots (NYT), and the next day voted to downgrade COVID-19 vaccination for adults under 65 from routine to 'shared clinical decision-making' (NPR). Through the fall, a new ACIP workgroup began examining vaccine timing and ingredients including aluminum, with Robert Malone and allies pushing to delay the newborn hepatitis B vaccine (The Hill, Oct 2025). In December 2025, Kennedy elevated Martin Kulldorff to a senior HHS science role and installed Malone and Kirk Milhoan on ACIP itself (Bloomberg, Dec 2025); days later the new panel chair -- a vaccine-skeptic cardiologist -- was reported to have described himself and fellow committee members as 'puppets on a string' on a private call, shortly after the panel's first action dropped the newborn hepatitis B recommendation (WSJ, Dec 2025). By February 2026, Milhoan, by then ACIP's chair, was publicly questioning the continued need for polio and MMR vaccination and calling school vaccine mandates 'authoritarian' (The Hill, Feb 3, 2026) -- the immediate policy backdrop against which the March 16, 2026 lawsuit and ruling below occurred.

Kennedy dismissed the existing members of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) and replaced them with appointees critical of or lacking expertise in vaccines. Six medical organizations sued, and on March 16, 2026, a federal judge ordered the reversal of all decisions made by the Kennedy-appointed ACIP panelists, finding the government had disregarded the scientific method. Separately, Kennedy fired CDC Director Susan Monarez after she resisted his efforts to control vaccine guidance; her attorney said she was ousted for refusing to 'rubber stamp unscientific, reckless directives.' Internal HHS emails later released by Sen. Bernie Sanders showed Kennedy directly ordering the CDC to pull flu vaccine ad campaigns and restrict vaccine access. Update: NBC News reported that as a direct consequence of the March 16, 2026 ruling, planned federal guidance for this fall's flu and COVID-19 vaccines was left in limbo, with Trump officials undecided as of the reporting whether to appeal. With CDC still lacking a Senate-confirmed director (documented separately in this tracker's Government Services database, cdc-leadership-vacancy-crisis-2026.json) and core ACIP advisory functions effectively frozen by the ruling, doctors quoted by NBC warned that routine public health guidance-setting was grinding to a halt at a time when clear guidance for the upcoming respiratory-illness season was needed. Update: In response to the March 16, 2026 ruling that his ACIP appointees were unqualified and the panel unlawfully reconstituted, Kennedy moved to rewrite ACIP's own membership charter, broadening the eligibility criteria for panel membership in a way that makes it easier to appoint members without traditional vaccine expertise -- addressing the court's specific finding by changing the rules governing who can qualify, rather than by appointing more conventionally credentialed members under the existing rules.

offense_category: Hatch Act Violation -- using the authority of a federal office to influence the outcome of an election by pressuring third-party candidates to withdraw from congressional races
incident_summary: Sen. Ron Wyden filed a complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel (OSC) alleging that HHS Secretary Robert F. Donald Sherman, president of the nonpartisan watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW), reviewed a recording of at least one call and said Kennedy invoked his official position and responsibilities as HHS Secretary multiple times during the conversation, calling it a 'clear violation' of the Hatch Act warranting OSC investigation. The complaint seeks an OSC investigation into whether Kennedy improperly used his cabinet position to influence the composition of two competitive U.S. House races. Trump has separately taken steps during his second term to assert greater control over OSC, including firing the office's head earlier in the term, raising questions about whether the currently constituted office will investigate the complaint independently.

The Office of Special Counsel is institutionally positioned to investigate and act on the complaint independently of the administration

incident_summary: On February 20, 2025, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a new presidential commission -- part of his 'Make America Healthy Again' (MAHA) initiative -- to investigate the childhood vaccine schedule, pesticides, psychiatric drugs, and other factors he framed as contributors to chronic childhood disease. The announcement drew scrutiny because it came despite assurances Kennedy had given during his confirmation process that he would not seek to undermine public confidence in existing, well-established vaccines. This commission is the earliest-dated action in what became a documented, escalating chain of vaccine-policy actions this tracker follows separately in later entries -- including a January 2026 immunization-schedule overhaul and the May 2026 Executive Order 14407 realigning the childhood vaccine schedule based on a December 2025 HHS assessment. Round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0367: the commission's own first deliverable undercut its credibility on release. Its 'Make America Healthy Again' assessment report, published in late May 2025, was found by NOTUS, Rolling Stone, ABC News, and PolitiFact to contain at least seven citations to studies that do not exist -- fabricated titles and authors bearing the hallmarks of generative-AI output -- plus other citations that misrepresented real studies' actual findings. Dr. Katherine Keyes, cited as the first author of a paper on teen depression/anxiety rates, confirmed to ABC News she never wrote it; the American Academy of Pediatrics and JAMA Pediatrics both told ABC News they could not locate certain cited papers in their own publication records. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt attributed the errors to 'some formatting issues' while stating the administration had 'complete confidence' in Kennedy's team; Kennedy himself called the fabricated citations a 'mistake.' House Oversight Committee Democrats, led by Rep. Stephen Lynch, sent HHS a formal letter on June 2, 2025 seeking an accounting of how the errors occurred and what if any AI tools were used in drafting the report.

incident_summary: AP reported May 15, 2025 that Trump's Surgeon General nominee, Dr. Casey Means -- a close ally of HHS Secretary Robert F. Means's confirmation hearing before the Senate HELP Committee was initially postponed after she went into labor, and was ultimately held February 25, 2026, where she was pressed on vaccine skepticism. Former Trump-administration Surgeon General Jerome Adams publicly said in a STAT News piece that Means 'does not meet basic standards' for the role. The nomination stalled in the Senate through early 2026 without a committee vote being scheduled, and on April 30, 2026, Trump withdrew it, nominating Dr. Nicole Saphier -- a board-certified radiologist and Fox News Channel contributor -- as his new Surgeon General pick instead.

incident_summary: In April 2025, Sali Berisha -- Albania's indicted former president and prime minister, barred from the U.S. since 2021 under Section 7031(c) of the State Department's annual appropriations act over Biden-era State Department findings that he misappropriated public funds to enrich relatives -- signed a two-year, $6 million lobbying contract with Continental Strategy, a Republican consulting firm. Continental's roster included Chris LaCivita (a co-manager of Trump's 2024 campaign), Alberto Martinez (a former chief of staff to then-Senator Rubio), and Katie Wiles (daughter of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, though AP reporting specifically found she was not staffed on the Berisha account). The Associated Press reported the arrangement was funded in part through a New Jersey-based group called the 'Make Albania Great Again Foundation,' whose donors were not publicly disclosed at the time. A little over a year later, on June 12, 2026, the State Department confirmed it had issued a waiver lifting Berisha's Section 7031(c) 'persona non grata' designation following what it described as an in-depth case review, restoring his and his family's ability to travel to the U.S. Berisha, announcing the reversal himself, credited Secretary of State Rubio personally, telling Albania's parliament 'I am back.' No sourcing reviewed directly quotes Rubio or any other State Department official connecting the lobbying campaign to the waiver decision, and none of the outlets covering the June 2026 reversal itself mention Continental Strategy or the lobbying contract at all -- the connection here is a documented, well-sourced temporal and access relationship (a paid lobbying campaign built specifically around Trump-administration proximity, followed just over a year later by exactly the sanctions reversal it was hired to obtain), not a proven quid pro quo.

incident_summary: In 2016, Dahud Hanid Ortiz -- a U.S. military veteran and dual Venezuelan-American citizen -- killed two Cuban women and an Ecuadorian man at a law office in Madrid, Spain, and fled to Venezuela afterward. Spain convicted him in absentia and requested his extradition, but Venezuela's constitution bars extraditing its own citizens, so Venezuela prosecuted him itself: he was arrested in 2018 and sentenced by a Caracas court on January 9, 2024 to 30 years in prison. In 2023, the Biden administration, aware of Ortiz's criminal record, chose not to include him when it negotiated a different prisoner swap with Venezuela that year. On July 18, 2025, the Trump administration completed a three-way exchange: El Salvador returned roughly 250 Venezuelan migrants to Venezuela -- men the U.S. had deported under the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 and paid El Salvador to hold at the CECOT mega-prison -- and in return Venezuela released 10 Americans (five citizens and five green-card holders), including Ortiz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly announced the released Americans were "on their way to freedom." Of the 10 people released, 8 were officially classified by the U.S. government as "wrongfully detained" -- the stated criterion used to justify prioritizing Americans for return -- but Ortiz was not among them. The New York Times reported that at least some people in the Trump administration knew of Ortiz's murder conviction before he was included in the swap, and Venezuela's Justice Minister, Diosdado Cabello, publicly confirmed U.S. officials were told of the conviction and still wanted him released. No U.S. official has since explained, on the record, why a convicted violent felon who did not meet the swap's own wrongful-detention criterion was included. Ortiz has been reported living freely in Orlando, Florida since his return.

Ortiz was not one of the 8 Americans in the same July 18, 2025 swap officially classified as "wrongfully detained," the criterion the administration publicly used to justify the exchange

The 2023 Biden administration, aware of the same criminal record, chose not to include Ortiz in a different prisoner swap that year, establishing that declining to include him was an available, previously-exercised option rather than an unavoidable condition of dealing with Venezuela

No U.S. official has publicly identified who made the decision to include Ortiz or explained the reasoning, leaving the process by which a non-wrongfully-detained convicted felon was selected for release undisclosed

incident_summary: Beginning in 2025, Rubio simultaneously held Secretary of State plus, at various points, Acting National Security Advisor, Acting Archivist of the United States, and Acting USAID Administrator. status: Threatened/under review -- State Department and DHS reviewing cases; no denaturalization proceeding against a Somali-American tied to this announcement had been filed as of this writing
incident_summary: On January 13, 2026, at a speech to the Detroit Economic Club, Trump said his administration would revoke the citizenship of naturalized Americans 'from Somalia or anywhere else' convicted of defrauding U.S. citizens, attributing much of a large Minnesota public-benefits fraud scandal to people who 'came into the country illegally from Somalia' -- despite the fraud defendants being predominantly naturalized citizens or lawful residents, not people who entered illegally. In earlier remarks (reported by Al Jazeera in late December 2025 and by The Hill), White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed the administration was 'looking at' revoking citizenship specifically for Somali-Americans caught up in the fraud scheme, and that DHS and the State Department were jointly reviewing what steps would be needed. Trump separately told reporters he would denaturalize citizens 'in a heartbeat' if they were 'dishonest,' and said of Somali immigrants specifically that 'many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.' The underlying Minnesota fraud scandal -- the Feeding Our Future child-nutrition-program scheme, the largest pandemic-relief fraud case charged in U.S. history at roughly $250 million, plus related autism-services and Housing Stabilization Program fraud bringing the total scope toward $822 million-$1 billion -- has produced 78 defendants charged and 56 convictions as of this writing; the U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota has stated approximately 89% of those charged are Somali-American. The administration's denaturalization threat invokes a real, pre-existing DOJ policy: a June 11, 2025 Civil Division memorandum signed by Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate directing attorneys to 'prioritize and maximally pursue denaturalization proceedings in all cases permitted by law,' listing fraud against private individuals, businesses, or the government as one of ten priority categories, alongside national-security threats and human-rights violations -- a facially neutral, nationality-blind policy. Legal experts, including immigration attorneys and civil-liberties groups (ACLU), argue that publicly announcing and reviewing denaturalization specifically for one national-origin group, rather than applying the same fraud-based criteria neutrally across all naturalized citizens convicted of similar conduct, raises equal-protection concerns distinct from the underlying policy's facial neutrality. Separately, ABC News reported DHS announced termination of Temporary Protected Status for Somalis in the same period this group was being publicly targeted by Trump -- a related but distinct DHS action affecting a different, non-citizen population.

official: Leland Dudek, Acting Commissioner of the Social Security Administration

incident_summary: On March 5, 2025, Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek ordered the cancellation of the agency's longstanding contracts with the State of Maine that automatically processed Social Security numbers for newborns at hospitals and death certificates from funeral homes -- contracts that, if actually terminated, would have forced Maine parents to travel to a federal Social Security office in person to register a newborn. official: John Thune, Senate Majority Leader
offense_category: Inserting an Undisclosed Self-Benefiting Provision Into Must-Pass Government Funding Legislation, Creating a Personal Financial Remedy for Himself and Colleagues Whose Records Were Lawfully Subpoenaed in a Federal Investigation
incident_summary: In November 2025, as Congress finalized the legislative package ending the 43-day government shutdown, Senate Majority Leader John Thune personally directed staff to insert language into one of the package's full-year spending bills allowing senators (and at least one House member) to sue the federal government for up to $500,000 in statutory damages per violation if their phone or electronic records were subpoenaed or obtained without their knowledge. The provision followed an October 2025 disclosure, via documents released by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, that then-Special Counsel Jack Smith's 2023 investigation into efforts to overturn the 2020 election had obtained phone records for eight Republican senators -- Lindsey Graham, Bill Hagerty, Josh Hawley, Dan Sullivan, Tommy Tuberville, Ron Johnson, Cynthia Lummis, and Marsha Blackburn -- around the time of the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, plus at least one House member, all via lawful grand jury subpoena. The provision was inserted without a standalone vote or public debate and signed into law along with the rest of the funding package. It drew immediate bipartisan criticism once discovered: House Speaker Mike Johnson said he was 'surprised and very frustrated,' calling it 'way out of line' and saying he was 'very angry about it'; Senate Finance Committee Democrat Ron Wyden called it a 'tax dollar giveaway to Republican senators.' Johnson announced the House would hold a standalone vote to strip the provision. The House did so, voting 426-0 to repeal the provision -- a second unanimous House repeal vote followed weeks later after the first stalled -- but Thune has refused to bring the repeal to a Senate floor vote, and Sen. Graham personally blocked a Democratic attempt to force one, arguing senators whose records were 'wrongly' obtained deserved a 'remedy.' As of this entry, the provision remains law, unrepealed, despite two unanimous House votes against it.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Categorical Clemency for 2020 Election-Subversion Co-Conspirators (Fake Electors, Legal Architects, and Aides), Issued via Sweeping, Ambiguously-Worded Proclamation Language -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pardon's non-individualized scale, its later-rejected attempted extension beyond its intended targets, and its practical inability to reach the parallel state prosecutions it was seemingly meant to shield.
incident_summary: On November 7, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation granting 'full, complete, and unconditional' federal pardons to 77 people over conduct connected to efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss; U.S. Pardon Attorney Ed Martin publicly released the list on November 10, 2025. Named recipients included Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani, former chief of staff Mark Meadows, attorney Sidney Powell, DOJ official-turned-elector-scheme architect Jeffrey Clark, and lawyers Kenneth Chesebro, Jenna Ellis, and John Eastman, alongside dozens of Republican 'fake electors' from Michigan, Arizona, Nevada, Georgia, and Wisconsin. The proclamation's operative language was sweeping rather than individualized, granting pardon for conduct relating to the 'advice, creation, organization, execution, submission, support, voting, activities, participation in, or advocacy for or of any slate or proposed slate of Presidential electors, whether or not recognized by any State or State official, in connection with the 2020 Presidential Election,' as well as for 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud and vulnerabilities in the 2020 Presidential Election.' Because the presidential pardon power under Article II reaches only federal offenses, and none of the named recipients had actually been charged with a federal crime over their 2020-election conduct (Special Counsel Jack Smith's federal case charged Trump himself, not these co-conspirators as defendants), the pardon left the parallel state prosecutions of many of the same people legally untouched: Georgia's 2023 racketeering indictment of Trump and 18 others (including Giuliani, Meadows, Chesebro, Ellis, and Eastman), Arizona's fake-elector indictment of 18 people, and Michigan's and Nevada's own fake-elector cases all continued under state authority the federal pardon has no power to reach. Legal scholars, including Loyola Law School's Justin Levitt (a former DOJ official), warned at the time that the proclamation's broad, non-individualized wording could unintentionally sweep in people Trump did not intend to cover. That warning proved accurate: Matthew Laiss, federally charged in September 2025 with double voting in the 2020 election (in person in Florida and by mail in Bucks County, Pennsylvania), invoked the proclamation's broad language as a defense. The Justice Department itself told the federal court it did not consider Laiss covered, stating it had consulted the Office of the Pardon Attorney and could 'explicitly confirm' Laiss fell outside the proclamation's intended scope. On January 13, 2026, a federal judge ruled the pardon did not apply to Laiss, finding he had not applied for or received the pardon certificate the proclamation's own terms require; Laiss was subsequently found guilty of the underlying voter-fraud charge. A second test case produced the opposite outcome. Harrison Floyd -- an ex-Marine and MMA fighter who worked on Trump's 2020 campaign, one of the 79 people actually named on the November pardon list for his role in the Georgia fake-electors racketeering case -- separately faced a federal charge from a February 2023 incident in which he allegedly rushed at and assaulted two FBI agents (spitting in their faces, per reporting) sent by then-Special Counsel Jack Smith to serve him a subpoena in the federal 2020-election-subversion investigation, an incident with no direct connection to the fake-electors conduct itself. Floyd's attorney, Carlos Salvado, told ABC News in November 2025 the pardon's broad 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud' language might extend to the unrelated assault charge, saying only 'there is an argument.' Unlike the Laiss case, DOJ did not contest the extension: on January 7, 2026, federal prosecutors moved to dismiss the assault charge, a decision reporting tied directly to the clemency order -- meaning the same ambiguous pardon language a federal judge rejected as a shield for Laiss's unrelated voter-fraud conviction was, weeks later, allowed by DOJ itself to end a federal prosecution for physically assaulting FBI agents in the line of duty.

status: The pardon proclamation is final and cannot itself be reversed. The state prosecutions it left unaffected -- including Georgia's racketeering case and Arizona's, Michigan's, and Nevada's fake-elector cases -- remained ongoing under state authority as of this writing. offense_category: Using Official U.S. Trade and Sanctions Authority to Attempt to Shield a Foreign Political Ally From a Legitimate Foreign Prosecution -- not itself a domestic criminal charge, addressed here as a foreign-policy/abuse-of-power accountability concern
incident_summary: In a July 9, 2025 letter to Brazil, Trump threatened a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods, explicitly citing and denouncing the ongoing coup-plot prosecution of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro -- an ally Trump has publicly supported -- as a politically motivated 'witch hunt.' Trump followed through by executive order, imposing a 40% additional tariff (bringing total duties on many Brazilian goods to 50%) and separately invoking the Global Magnitsky Act -- a sanctions law designed for human-rights abusers and corrupt officials -- against Alexandre de Moraes, the Brazilian Supreme Court justice overseeing the Bolsonaro case, freezing his U.S.-based assets and barring his travel to the United States. The administration also revoked U.S. visas for 8 of Brazil's 11 Supreme Court justices and other Brazilian officials, including the health minister. Despite this pressure campaign, Brazil's Supreme Court proceeded to sentence Bolsonaro to 27 years in prison on September 11, 2025, citing 'overwhelming evidence' including assassination plans against President Lula and Justice Moraes drafted inside the presidential palace. Brazilian President Lula publicly framed his government's refusal to intervene in the judiciary as a defense of national sovereignty, and his domestic popularity rose amid the confrontation, while Brazil simultaneously expanded trade ties with China as U.S.-Brazil relations strained. In November 2025, Trump signed an executive order exempting coffee, beef, and other agricultural products from the 40% tariff, and relations improved further after an October 2025 Trump-Lula meeting at the ASEAN summit, which Lula described as 'surprisingly good,' with Trump reportedly assuring him a broader trade agreement could be reached. By mid-2026, however, a new dispute emerged: Trump proposed a fresh 25% tariff on Brazilian products, which became entangled with Brazil's 2026 presidential race after Bolsonaro's son, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro (a 2026 presidential candidate), publicly asked Trump to delay the tariffs until after the election, while Lula separately pushed back against the proposal. Added 2026-09-10 (round-4 backlog cluster c0581): this Brazil-specific pressure campaign was part of a broader pattern -- see the companion entry trump-foreign-judiciary-sanctions-pattern-2025.json, which documents parallel U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and its judges over the Netanyahu/Gallant arrest warrants, and informal pressure on France over Marine Le Pen's conviction.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Presidential Pardon of Political Allies Convicted of Federal Corruption, Accompanied by a Factually False 'Biden Over-Prosecution' Narrative -- clemency is a constitutional power, not itself unlawful; the accountability question is the falsity of the administration's own stated justification for it
incident_summary: Former Tennessee House Speaker Glen Casada and his top aide Cade Cothren were convicted on 17 federal charges, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering, for operating a fake consulting firm ('Phoenix Solutions,' run under the false identity 'Matthew Phoenix') that funneled taxpayer and campaign money -- including a $52,000 legislator-mailer program -- back to themselves. Casada was sentenced to 36 months in prison in September 2025; Cothren received a shorter sentence. On November 10, 2025, Trump granted both men pardons. A White House official justified the pardons by claiming 'the Biden Department of Justice significantly over-prosecuted these individuals for a minor issue involving constituent mailers -- which were billed at competitive prices, never received a complaint from legislators, and resulted in a net profit loss of less than $5,000.' This framing is contradicted by the case's own timeline: the investigation began during Trump's first term, FBI raids on Casada's and Cothren's properties occurred in January 2021 while Trump was still president, and the judge who oversaw the case and sentenced Casada was a Trump first-term appointee -- meaning no part of the prosecution, investigation, or sentencing occurred under a Biden-appointed official or during the Biden administration's DOJ leadership.

On May 29, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14407, directing the CDC and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to realign the U.S. childhood vaccine schedule with a December 2025 HHS assessment. That assessment called for reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, reasoning that the U.S. recommends more childhood vaccines than 'peer nations' such as Denmark and more than twice as many vaccine doses as some European countries. official: Donald Trump, President (acting through the White House Office of Presidential Personnel); Peter Kirsanow, Commissioner, designated by the White House as replacement chair
offense_category: Attempted unilateral executive takeover of an independent, statutorily bipartisan watchdog commission, circumventing 42 U.S.C. § 1975's requirement that the President designate the Commission's chair only "with the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members" -- NOT charged; a political/institutional dispute, not a criminal matter
incident_summary: In April 2025, the White House sent a 'de-designation' email to Rochelle Garza, the Democratic chair of the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (a term she had held since March 17, 2023), seeking to demote her and elevate Republican commissioner Peter Kirsanow as the new chair. Garza refused to step down, citing 42 U.S.C. § 1975's requirement that a chair be designated only with the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members -- not by unilateral presidential letter -- and declined to recognize a vote on new leadership as procedurally in order. The White House renewed the attempt in March 2026, when the deputy director of the Office of Presidential Personnel sent a similar letter seeking the same change; Garza again resisted, and the Commission's own website continued to list her as chair as of at least June 12, 2026 (she is documented moderating an official Commission hearing on immigration enforcement in Minnesota that month). The dispute sits against the backdrop of a major, unrelated Supreme Court ruling: on June 29, 2026, the Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6-3, overruling the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor v. United States precedent and holding that for-cause removal protections for heads of independent multi-member agencies exercising executive power violate separation of powers. That case arose from Trump's firing of two Democratic FTC commissioners, not from the Civil Rights Commission, but its reasoning substantially strengthens the legal argument that Trump could lawfully remove or override Garza going forward -- a development not yet resolved as of this entry's creation.
elements_required: A specific statutory chair-designation process exists (42 U.S.C. § 1975: majority-of-commissioners concurrence required) that the White House's unilateral 'de-designation' letters did not follow
The White House made a direct, on-the-record attempt to replace Garza as chair outside that process, more than once
Garza's continued service as chair despite these attempts, as documented by the Commission's own public record

Whether Trump v. Slaughter's broader removal-power holding will be extended to override the Commission's own concurrence requirement remains an open legal question, not yet tested against this Commission specifically

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue that a president has broad authority to designate his preferred leadership of an executive-branch commission, that Kirsanow was already a sitting, Senate-relevant commissioner rather than an outside appointee, and that Trump v. comeback: The statute at issue is specific and unambiguous: 42 U.S.C. § 1975 conditions the President's chair-designation power on 'the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members,' precisely because Congress designed this particular commission -- capped at no more than 4 members from one party -- to resist unilateral partisan control. incident_summary: On August 11, 2025, President Trump announced he was placing Washington, D.C.'s Metropolitan Police Department under direct federal control and deploying the National Guard, invoking Section 740 of the D.C. Home Rule Act to declare a 'crime emergency.' Within about a week, roughly 800 D.C. National Guard troops had been mobilized, with additional state National Guard units en route, alongside roughly 500 newly deployed immigration and other federal agents patrolling the streets and operating checkpoints. Trump characterized the city as suffering 'bloodshed and squalor,' but the city's own crime data showed violent crime had been declining for two consecutive years before the declaration: homicides fell 32% in 2024 (from a 2023 peak of 274, the city's highest since 1997, to 187) and continued falling roughly 12% further into 2025. D.C. officials and local commentators characterized the declared emergency as a pretext rather than a response to worsening conditions, noting the administration's own policies had simultaneously strained the district's justice system -- including a purge of senior federal prosecutors who had worked on January 6 cases (documented separately in this database's ed-martin-jan6-prosecutor-purge-hale-cusanelli-2025.json) and a years-long judgeship vacancy crisis at the D.C. Superior Court, which as of 2025 remained understaffed against its 62-judge target even as Senate confirmation of backlogged nominees continued; Superior Court felony case filings rose 44% in 2025, coinciding with the administration's push for increased federal prosecutions in the district. Added 2026-09-12 (round-4 backlog cluster c0567): Reuters reported (September 4, 2025, based on interviews with nine current and former FBI employees) that the surge pulled FBI agents who normally work out of the public eye into visible street patrols and checkpoint duty in unmarked vehicles -- as many as 1,000 unmarked FBI cars were used in Washington during the highly public deployment. FBI employees said the exposure risked burning vehicles the bureau relies on for undercover work against cartels, violent gangs, and foreign intelligence services; one employee said, 'We can't use these cars to go undercover, we can't use them to surveil narcotraffickers and fentanyl suppliers or Russian or Chinese spies or use them to go after violent criminal gangs or terrorists.' The surge, justified by the administration as a violent-crime crackdown, drew criticism for featuring many arrests for minor offenses while creating this operational-security cost to the FBI's own national-security and counterintelligence capacity.
elements_required: Section 740 of the D.C. Home Rule Act authorizes the President to direct the Mayor to provide D.C. police services for federal purposes he determines are of a special nature and emergency circumstance, but was designed around brief, narrowly-defined emergencies -- its application here to a broad, open-ended 'crime emergency' declaration is the contested legal question, not a settled violation

The declared factual predicate (an ongoing crime crisis) is directly contradicted by the district's own published crime statistics, which showed two consecutive years of declining violent crime, including a 32% homicide drop in 2024 and continued decline into 2025

The scale of the federal response -- ~800 National Guard troops and ~500 federal agents -- and its timing followed, rather than preceded, documented administration-driven strain on D.C.'s own justice-system capacity (prosecutor purges, judgeship vacancies)

incident_summary: On March 25, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14248, 'Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections,' which sought to require documentary proof of citizenship for federal voter registration, directed the Department of Homeland Security (with the Social Security Administration) to compile state-by-state citizenship lists, and directed states to reject mail/absentee ballots received after Election Day even if postmarked on time. Military-family voting advocates joined a lawsuit challenging the order in April 2025, arguing the postmark/receipt-deadline change and citizenship-documentation requirements would disproportionately disenfranchise servicemembers and their families stationed abroad or deployed, who already face mail delays military voters have long relied on postmark-based deadlines to accommodate. Multiple federal courts subsequently ruled against key provisions: a coalition of 19 state attorneys general won a permanent injunction in the District of Massachusetts blocking the citizenship-documentation and mail-ballot-deadline provisions, and a separate ruling permanently blocked the provision requiring the Election Assistance Commission to mandate proof-of-citizenship documents on the federal voter registration form. In August 2026, the Supreme Court handed Trump a procedural win, staying the injunction 6-3 ahead of the November 2026 midterms -- but on standing grounds, finding the states had sued too early and had not yet shown concrete harm, not on the merits of whether the order itself is constitutional. A separate nationwide ruling by a U.S. District Judge in Boston continues to block the U.S. Postal Service specifically from following the order's mail-ballot directives.

offense_category: Rescission of Executive-Branch Ethics Pledge Requirements (Lobbyist Gift Ban and Revolving-Door Restriction) -- no criminal or civil legal violation established; the accountability concern is the removal of a structural anti-corruption safeguard rather than any single unlawful act
incident_summary: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed Executive Order 14148, rescinding a list of Biden-era executive orders and actions, including Executive Order 13989. That Biden order had required every executive-branch appointee to sign an ethics pledge committing them not to accept gifts from lobbyists or lobbying organizations, and imposing a two-year 'revolving door' ban preventing new appointees from working on regulations or contracts tied to their immediately prior employer or clients. Rescinding it removed both restrictions for Trump's incoming appointees. One immediate documented effect was that former Biden-administration appointees, no longer bound by the two-year post-employment restriction that had applied to them, were freed to move quickly into lobbying jobs. As of this entry's research, Trump had not issued a replacement ethics pledge or comparable restriction of his own for his administration's appointees, despite this being a step new administrations have typically taken.

No replacement ethics-pledge requirement or comparable restriction had been issued as of contemporaneous reporting

offense_category: Apparent Quid Pro Quo -- a $5 million campaign donation followed within weeks by the President's personal intervention to delay a federal agency's regulatory action benefiting the donor, raising accountability concerns under anti-corruption norms even absent a criminal bribery charge, which requires proof of an explicit agreed exchange not established here
status: Rule delay remained in effect as of this entry's last-verified date, with implementation pushed to at least January 1, 2026; Extremity Care's principal donor made a second, larger ($2.5 million, initially anonymous) donation to Trump's White House ballroom project in October 2025
incident_summary: Extremity Care LLC, which sells 'skin substitute' wound-care products made from placental and other tissue, donated $5 million to the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. super PAC on February 24, 2025 -- a donation not publicly disclosed until July 31, 2025, buried on page 18 of the PAC's mid-year filing. The Biden administration had proposed a CMS rule limiting Medicare coverage of skin substitutes to products 'supported by evidence' of effectiveness, which CMS itself found would have excluded 92% of currently covered products (identifying only 17 with proven scientific validity) -- including Extremity Care's, which cost $7,812 to $11,051 per square inch, compared to $75 to $195 for proven alternatives. Days after the donation, Extremity Care co-owner Oliver Burckhardt attended a Mar-a-Lago donor dinner and spoke with Trump. The next morning, March 1, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social attacking the rule and claiming, without evidentiary support, that it would cause '431,429 lost limbs annually and 187,286 additional deaths.' CMS, which had already pushed the rule's original effective date from February to April 13, 2025, announced on April 11, 2025 -- 40 days after Trump's post -- a further delay to at least January 1, 2026. Between April and July 2025 alone, Medicare spent an additional $2.3 billion on skin substitutes while the rule remained blocked, on top of a broader spending surge in the category from a negligible amount in 2014 to more than $10 billion in 2024. Extremity Care separately retained Trump fundraiser Brian Ballard as a lobbyist for $320,000 annually; Ballard's former employee, Susie Wiles, is Trump's White House Chief of Staff. In October 2025, Burckhardt attended a second Trump donor dinner, this one at the White House Rose Garden, and the New York Times later reported Extremity Care had been an anonymous $2.5 million donor to Trump's White House ballroom construction fund.

The President's own social-media statement opposing the rule, containing specific numerical claims (limb-loss and death figures) that lack cited evidentiary support
A federal agency (CMS) action -- a further implementation delay -- following within 40 days of the President's public position, benefiting the donor commercially
A quantified financial benefit to the donor and cost to the Medicare program ($2.3 billion in additional spending over roughly three months) resulting from the delay
A second, larger donation from the same donor to a Trump-connected fund (the White House ballroom) later in 2025, initially undisclosed, suggesting a continuing pattern rather than an isolated event

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Executive Order Stripping Collective Bargaining Rights From Two-Thirds of the Federal Workforce, Upheld on Appeal Over a Retaliation Challenge -- documents a contested but now judicially-sustained administration action, not an allegation of illegality
incident_summary: Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0503, 7 of 8 records): this entry previously skipped from the order's issuance straight to its 2026 appellate history, with no account of the order's specifics or its agency-by-agency rollout. President Trump signed the underlying order -- Executive Order 14251, 'Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs' -- on March 27, 2025, excluding roughly 40 agencies and subdivisions across 18 federal departments (including Defense, State, Treasury, HHS, and Veterans Affairs) from the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute on stated national-security grounds. A federal judge (Donato, below) initially blocked the order in April 2025, but after courts allowed enforcement to proceed, agencies moved through August 2025 to terminate union contracts covering hundreds of thousands of workers in quick succession: the EPA ended contracts with AFGE and four other unions on August 19, 2025; USDA moved August 24, 2025 to end union representation for roughly 6,500 FSIS food-safety inspectors and 1,650 APHIS plant-health inspectors, prompting a separate union lawsuit arguing that inspection work has nothing to do with national security; and by August 31, 2025, VA, EPA, and Agriculture Department contracts had all been voided in the same wave (VA's termination specifically is documented in greater depth in this tracker's collins-va-union-contempt-defiance-2026.json). Trump then expanded the order's scope: Executive Order 14343, 'Further Exclusions From the Federal Labor-Management Relations Program,' signed August 28, 2025 (published in the Federal Register September 3, 2025), added agencies including NASA, the Patent and Trademark Office, and the National Weather Service -- NASA's own implementation notice confirmed the agency would stop recognizing certain unions as exclusive bargaining representatives and halt collection of union dues on their behalf. On September 25, 2025, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III terminated the agency's collective bargaining agreement covering more than 30,000 of its roughly 34,900 employees, represented by the Council of Prison Locals/AFGE, calling the union 'an obstacle to progress instead of a partner in it.' In Congress, a bipartisan effort to protect Defense Department civilians' bargaining rights via the FY2026 NDAA -- which had passed the House 231-196 in September 2025 -- was stripped from the final compromise bill in December 2025; only Sen. Lisa Murkowski among Senate Republicans publicly pushed to keep the provision, unsuccessfully. Separately, the House later passed standalone legislation (unrelated to the NDAA) to restore collective bargaining rights for the affected workforce, with sponsors describing it as covering close to a million workers -- consistent with, though somewhat higher than, this entry's own two-thirds-of-the-federal-workforce figure for the executive order's reach; the bill's Senate fate was not resolved as of this update. In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order eliminating collective bargaining rights for wide swaths of the federal workforce, citing national security grounds. Federal employee unions sued, arguing the order was actually issued to retaliate against unions for challenging other administration policies, in violation of their free-speech rights; U.S. District Judge James Donato in San Francisco temporarily blocked the order. On appeal, a three-judge panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed Donato's injunction on February 26, 2026, finding the order was legitimately grounded in national security concerns and that Trump would have taken the same action regardless of any intent to punish the unions -- rejecting the retaliation theory. The 9th Circuit had already paused Donato's block pending the appeal's outcome since August 2025. The ruling affects an estimated two-thirds of the federal civilian workforce's bargaining rights.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Using U.S. Sanctions Authority to Punish or Pressure Foreign Judges and Courts Over Rulings Against Political Allies -- a pattern spanning the ICC, Brazil, and France, not itself a domestic criminal charge
incident_summary: Beyond the Brazil-specific sanctions on Justice Alexandre de Moraes over the Bolsonaro prosecution -- documented in full in this database's trump-brazil-tariffs-bolsonaro-protection-2025.json entry -- Trump's administration built a broader pattern of using U.S. sanctions authority against foreign judiciaries whose rulings affected political allies. On February 6, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14203 authorizing sanctions against the International Criminal Court and its Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan, in response to ICC arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. In June 2025, Secretary of State Rubio named four sitting ICC judges for sanctions -- Beti Hohler (Slovenia), Reine Alapini-Gansou (Benin), Luz del Carmen Ibanez Carranza (Peru), and Solome Bossa (Uganda) -- two of whom had participated in the proceedings leading to the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants; a U.S. federal judge later blocked domestic enforcement of the sanctions. The ICC, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch condemned the sanctions as an attack on international judicial independence; further sanctions on the ICC's president and a senior prosecution lawyer followed in 2026. Separately, after a French court convicted National Rally leader Marine Le Pen of embezzling European Union funds and barred her from running for office (March 31, 2025), Trump publicly demanded France 'free Marine Le Pen' and called her office ban 'a very big deal.' French magistrate Magali Lafourcade said she reported to French authorities that Trump administration emissaries had approached her in May 2025 attempting to characterize Le Pen's prosecution as purely political; no formal U.S. sanctions against French judges were identified in sourcing reviewed, distinguishing this instance from the more formal ICC and Brazil actions. Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, cluster c0806): fuller reporting on this same May 2025 episode, published by AFP and picked up by the Irish Times and Newsweek in January 2026, identified Lafourcade specifically as secretary general of France's National Advisory Commission on Human Rights (CNCDH) and quoted her directly: the two Trump advisers steered a Paris meeting that began on general human-rights topics toward Le Pen's case, seeking 'elements indicating that this was a purely political trial to stop her running for president.' Lafourcade said she immediately reported the exchange to the French foreign ministry -- an unusual step for CNCDH, which she said does not normally report its diplomatic exchanges given its institutional independence -- specifically out of concern it could constitute 'manipulation of the public debate in France.' A Washington Post report (Sept. 12, 2025) characterized the combined pattern across these countries as Trump 'escalating his war on the judiciary overseas,' with the White House framing the actions as defending free speech and political allies while experts said they undercut judicial independence norms globally.

incident_summary: On November 13, 2024, President-elect Trump nominated former Rep. Matt Gaetz to be Attorney General, the nation's top law-enforcement post overseeing federal sex-trafficking and civil-rights enforcement. Gaetz had faced a federal sex-trafficking investigation beginning in 2021 -- DOJ ultimately declined to bring charges -- but the House Committee on Ethics had separately been conducting its own investigation, effectively derailed when Gaetz resigned from the House the day after his nomination. The Ethics Committee nonetheless later released its findings, concluding there was 'substantial evidence' Gaetz violated Florida's statutory rape laws, among other findings. Newly unsealed court records reported by the New York Times on November 13, 2025 (one year after the nomination) detailed the vulnerable circumstances of the minor victim at the center of the case: she was a homeless high school junior living in a shelter with a parent, working at McDonald's, who joined a 'sugar dating' website in an effort to save money for braces, falsely listing her age as 18. She testified she met Gaetz in December 2016, at age 17, through Joel Greenberg -- a Gaetz associate later convicted in a broader sex-trafficking scheme -- and that Gaetz paid her for sex. Gaetz has consistently denied the allegations, telling the Times the account was 'fiction' and that he 'never had sex with this person,' who he said had instead threatened to sue him for $2.3 million. Gaetz withdrew his AG nomination on November 22, 2024, nine days after it was announced, citing a desire to avoid becoming 'a needlessly protracted Washington scuffle' and 'a distraction' to the transition; CNN and other outlets reported the more direct proximate cause was that Trump personally told Gaetz he lacked the Senate votes for confirmation, amid senators' concerns over the same allegations.

incident_summary: On January 28, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14187, 'Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation,' directing federal agencies to withhold grant funding from medical institutions that provide gender-affirming care -- including puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and certain surgical procedures -- to patients under 19, and directing exclusion of these treatments from Tricare (military health coverage) and calling for restrictions under Medicare and Medicaid. The order was challenged almost immediately: Lambda Legal filed suit on behalf of PFLAG in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland on February 4, 2025, and on March 4, 2025 the court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction barring the federal government from withholding funding from institutions on the basis that they provide this care to minors. The order has not been enforceable since that injunction. A second front opened in late 2025: a coalition of 19 states and the District of Columbia sued HHS and other federal defendants, filing a motion for summary judgment on January 6, 2026 that challenged an HHS report (referred to in litigation as the 'Kennedy Declaration,' after HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) cited to justify the restrictions; at oral argument on March 19, 2026 the presiding judge indicated an intent to partially grant the states' request to invalidate that declaration.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Presidential Imposition of an Unauthorized Tax Via Proclamation -- a federal court found the $100,000 H-1B visa fee exceeded executive authority, violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and violated separation-of-powers principles by usurping Congress's exclusive taxing authority
incident_summary: In September 2025, Trump announced by proclamation a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, dramatically increasing the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers. A coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general sued, and on June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston ruled the fee unlawful, finding it constituted a tax Trump imposed without congressional authorization -- an authority the Constitution reserves to Congress -- and that the administration's implementation violated both the Administrative Procedure Act and constitutional separation-of-powers principles. Despite the ruling, the court's order blocking the fee was temporarily paused on June 12, 2026 to allow an appeals court to consider the government's request for a stay; as a result, USCIS remained permitted to continue collecting the $100,000 fee pending appeal even after a federal court found it unlawful. Update 2026-08-18: this entry's original status line -- that the fee "remained collectible pending appeal" -- was already out of date by its own August 2, 2026 write date. On July 24, 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government's request to stay Judge Sorokin's ruling, finding the administration had not shown it was likely to succeed on the merits; as a result, the fee has been unenforceable nationwide since that denial. Separately, a different lawsuit (brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities) produced the opposite result: the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia upheld the fee, creating a direct circuit-level conflict now pending before the D.C. Circuit (oral argument held March 2026, no ruling identified as of this update). As of August 12, 2026 reporting, the administration was expected to seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court but had not yet filed such an application.

official: Donald Trump, President of the United States
offense_category: 26 U.S.C. § 7217 -- federal law making it a felony for the President or other executive branch officials to request the IRS conduct, terminate, or otherwise influence an audit or investigation of a specific, named taxpayer
status: Threatened repeatedly (April 2025, renewed publicly May 2, 2025) but not formally carried out as of last verification -- no sourcing reviewed confirms the IRS actually opened a revocation proceeding or issued a final determination against Harvard's tax-exempt status
incident_summary: After Harvard rejected a series of Trump administration demands in an April 11, 2025 letter -- including governance and leadership changes, altered hiring and admissions practices, and ending DEI programs -- Trump signaled on April 16, 2025 that he wanted Harvard to lose its tax-exempt status, and multiple outlets (Washington Post, CNN, Inside Higher Ed) reported the same day that the administration had directly asked the IRS to revoke it. Legal experts immediately flagged that this appeared to violate 26 U.S.C. § 7217, the statute Congress passed specifically to bar the President and other officials from directing the IRS to investigate or act against a named taxpayer -- a George Mason University tax law professor said he was unaware of any prior administration attempting something like this. Harvard filed suit April 21, 2025 to halt a related federal funding freeze, and Harvard President Alan Garber publicly called the tax-exempt threat 'highly illegal.' Trump renewed the threat publicly on May 2, 2025, saying revocation was 'what they deserve.' Reporting in 2025-2026 indicates the Treasury Department separately made an inquiry to the IRS's then-acting chief counsel, Andrew De Mello, regarding rescinding Harvard's status, and that a formal revocation would require the IRS to first open a full audit and issue notice to Harvard -- a process with no sourcing reviewed confirming it was ever formally initiated. Harvard's own communications office stated 'there is no legal basis to rescind Harvard's tax-exempt status.' This action ran concurrently with, but is legally and factually distinct from, the administration's separate SEVP-certification revocation (see noem-harvard-sevp-revocation-2025.json) and its $2.6 billion research-funding freeze (see harvard-research-funding-freeze-2025.json) against the same university.

Multiple independent outlets reported the administration directly asked the IRS to act on this specific request, which is the conduct 26 U.S.C. § 7217 was written to prohibit
The timing directly followed Harvard's public refusal of the administration's broader demands, supporting a retaliatory rather than a routine tax-enforcement motive
Legal experts and Harvard's own leadership publicly characterized the threat as illegal, not merely controversial

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Pardon Followed by Federal Bureau of Prisons Special-Treatment Assistance to a Convicted Foreign Drug Trafficker -- extends this tracker's pardon-power pattern (see trump-kidan-donor-pardon-2026.json) to include post-pardon logistical favoritism by a federal agency
incident_summary: On November 28, 2025, Trump announced he would pardon Juan Orlando Hernández, the former president of Honduras, who had been convicted by a U.S. federal jury in June 2024 on cocaine-trafficking-conspiracy and related firearms charges and sentenced to 45 years -- one of the most significant international narcotics prosecutions in DOJ history. Trump formally granted the pardon on December 1, 2025, and Hernández was released the same day. ProPublica's investigation found that despite Hernández having an active ICE immigration detainer in place at the time of his release -- a standard hold requiring law enforcement to turn a noncitizen over to ICE -- the Federal Bureau of Prisons scrambled to have the detainer lifted (records show it was removed just after 11 p.m. that night) so Hernández could walk free rather than be transferred to ICE custody. BOP then paid a four-person tactical team overtime to personally drive Hernández roughly six hours from a West Virginia high-security facility to the Waldorf Astoria hotel in Manhattan, rather than providing standard transportation. Immigration attorney Lena Graber told ProPublica, 'Most people with drug convictions would never get their ICE detainer removed just because the conviction was pardoned.' Added 2026-09-09 (round-4 backlog cluster c0735): Trump's November 28 pardon announcement came two days before Honduras's presidential election and was paired with an endorsement of Nasry 'Tito' Asfura -- the candidate of Hernández's own National Party -- with Trump saying 'Tito and I can work together to fight the narco-communists,' seemingly conditioning future U.S. support on an Asfura win. Trump justified the pardon by claiming Hernández had been 'treated very harshly and unfairly' and had been the victim of a 'Biden setup,' echoing a claim in Hernández's own letter to Trump that he had been politically persecuted by the Biden administration rather than legitimately prosecuted -- a characterization the underlying 2024 federal jury conviction on cocaine-trafficking and firearms charges directly contradicts. Farmers protested the pardon in Tegucigalpa on December 4, 2025, and on December 8, 2025, Honduras's attorney general ordered domestic authorities and asked Interpol to execute a previously-dormant 2023 Honduran arrest order against Hernández tied to the long-running 'Pandora' public-funds diversion case -- in which prosecutors allege a network of officials funneled government money through nongovernmental organizations to political campaigns, including roughly $2.3 million to Hernández's own 2013 presidential campaign. That reactivated arrest order and Interpol notice were not enforced while Hernández remained in the United States; a Honduran judge suspended both in mid-2026 at his lawyers' request, allowing him to return to Honduras on July 26, 2026, at which point the 'Pandora II' domestic prosecution this entry already tracks began in earnest.

BOP took affirmative steps to remove Hernández's active ICE detainer specifically because of the pardon, a step immigration law experts say is not standard practice for pardoned drug offenders
BOP provided bespoke, taxpayer-funded logistical assistance (a paid tactical-team drive to a luxury Manhattan hotel) rather than standard release procedures
This favorable treatment occurred contemporaneously with the administration's own mass ICE enforcement operations against far less serious immigration violators, documented elsewhere in this tracker

incident_summary: Trump nominated Paul Ingrassia, then DHS's White House liaison, to lead the Office of Special Counsel on May 29, 2025. offense_category: Unlawful Mass Removal of Inspectors General Without Statutorily Required Congressional Notice -- a federal court later found the firings violated the Inspector General Act, a civil/administrative legal violation, not a criminal one
incident_summary: On January 24, 2025, Trump fired inspectors general at 17 federal agencies in a single night, including at the Department of Labor and other major departments. The Inspector General Act of 1978, as amended in 2022, requires the President to give Congress 30 days' advance notice of an IG's removal along with substantive, case-specific reasons -- neither was provided. Sen. Jon Ossoff and other lawmakers immediately warned the firings violated federal law and demanded they be rescinded. Eight of the fired inspectors general sued on February 12, 2025, seeking reinstatement. On September 24, 2025, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes ruled the firings had in fact violated the law, but declined to order reinstatement, reasoning that Trump could simply re-fire the same inspectors general after providing the 30-day notice the law required the first time -- leaving the plaintiffs without a practical remedy despite winning on the merits. Separately, in October 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo overhauling the Pentagon's own inspector general complaint process, requiring complaints against senior officials to be deemed 'credible' within seven days of filing and directing that 'repeat complainants' be tracked -- changes oversight advocates said would discourage legitimate whistleblowing, coming as the broader 17-IG purge remained unremedied.

offense_category: Categorical Clemency for January 6 Capitol Attack Defendants, Including Violent-Offense and Seditious-Conspiracy Convictions, and Its Downstream Effects -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the scale/non-individualized nature of the grant, its erosion of the public case record, and the pattern of political and paramilitary rehabilitation it enabled
incident_summary: On January 20-21, 2025, his first full day in office, Trump issued clemency covering roughly 1,500-1,600 people charged or convicted over the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack -- pardons for most, and sentence commutations for several leaders of extremist groups convicted of seditious conspiracy, including Oath Keepers founder Stewart Rhodes. Many recipients had been convicted of violent offenses (assaulting police officers) or were leaders of the Oath Keepers and Proud Boys. Within days, DOJ took offline its searchable public database of January 6 case records (charges, evidence, sentences), making it substantially harder for the public to verify what exactly had been pardoned, even though press releases and court records remained technically accessible elsewhere. A senior DOJ prosecutor who had helped bring the cases, Michael Romano, resigned in protest, warning the pardons would embolden future right-wing political violence. Over the following year, several downstream effects were documented: pardoned Proud Boys leader Enrique Tarrio personally thanked Trump at Mar-a-Lago in May 2025 ('you saved my life'), and other pardoned defendants began appearing at Republican events and floating political runs; Trump's pardon attorney Ed Martin met in May 2025 with allies pushing for pardons covering the small remaining group of convicted January 6 defendants, including Rhodes and multiple Proud Boys leaders; by late 2025, Rhodes -- his sentence commuted -- was attempting to relaunch the Oath Keepers as an explicitly pro-Trump paramilitary organization, claiming the president could 'call us up' against 'left-wing insurrections' (though former members and donors showed little interest); in January 2026, legal experts flagged that the pardon proclamation's broad 'related to' language could be read to cover Brian Cole Jr., who planted pipe bombs near the Capitol the night before the riot, despite DOJ's own effort to prosecute that case as unrelated to January 6; and Adam Johnson, pardoned after being photographed carrying House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's lectern during the riot, filed to run for a Manatee County, Florida commission seat in January 2026, using the Capitol photo in his campaign branding.

incident_summary: Added 2026-09-11 (round-4 backlog fold, clusters c0661 and c0695): this entry documents at least three named, unrelated pardoned Jan. 6 defendants who committed serious new crimes after receiving clemency -- Christopher Moynihan (political violence, described below), John Banuelos (kidnapping/sexual assault, described further below), and Andrew Paul Johnson (child sex abuse, described further below), reported as part of a broader pattern of post-pardon recidivism. John Banuelos -- the only Jan. 6 defendant accused of firing a gun on Capitol grounds -- was charged in Utah on November 10, 2025 with aggravated kidnapping and aggravated sexual assault stemming from a June 2018 attack, after an August 2025 DNA test linked him to the assault. His federal Capitol riot case was dismissed and he was released from custody after Trump's January 20, 2025 clemency grant. During 2024 proceedings before his Jan. 6 case's judge, Tanya Chutkan, Banuelos said, 'Trump is going to be in office in six months, so I have nothing to worry about' -- an explicit anticipation of impunity voiced before the pardon was even granted. Christopher Moynihan, convicted in 2022 for obstructing an official proceeding after breaking through a security perimeter and entering the Senate Gallery on Jan. 6, 2021 (sentenced to nearly two years), received a full pardon within hours of Trump's inauguration in January 2025 along with over 1,500 other Jan. 6 defendants. On October 21, 2025, Moynihan was arrested and charged with making a terroristic threat after sending text messages on October 17, 2025 reading 'Hakeem Jeffries makes a speech in a few days in NYC I cannot allow this terrorist to live,' 'Even if I am hated he must be eliminated,' and 'I will kill him for the future,' referring to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries ahead of a scheduled New York speech. Reporting described him as the first pardoned Capitol rioter arrested over alleged political violence. Jeffries said he was 'grateful to state and federal law enforcement for their swift and decisive action to apprehend a dangerous individual'; Rep. Jamie Raskin said the case illustrated Trump granting pardons 'without obviously studying the details of each individual case.' Moynihan later pleaded guilty to a reduced misdemeanor harassment charge, with sentencing set for April 2026. Andrew Paul Johnson, who received a full pardon from President Trump for his role in the January 6, 2021 Capitol riot as part of Trump's blanket pardon of hundreds of Jan. 6 defendants in January 2025, was arrested in August 2025 -- roughly seven months after his pardon -- and subsequently convicted by a Hernando County, Florida jury in February 2026 on five felony charges, including molesting a child under 12, molesting a child under 16, and lewd and lascivious exhibition. Johnson was sentenced to life in prison in March 2026. Prosecutors said Johnson attempted to bribe one victim using money he claimed he would receive as restitution owed to Jan. 6 defendants. NPR's reporting characterized this as the latest in a documented pattern of pardoned Capitol rioters committing new crimes after receiving clemency.

Johnson was arrested for an unrelated, serious violent crime against children within months of receiving that pardon

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Privacy Act Violation (5 U.S.C. § 552a) -- unauthorized disclosure of protected personal records
incident_summary: On March 17, 2025, Trump ordered the immediate, unredacted release of all remaining classified John F. Kennedy assassination records, and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) published over 80,000 pages within about 24 hours -- bypassing the extensive review process NARA had previously used under the JFK Records Act to withhold Social Security numbers and other personal data of living individuals. The rushed release publicly exposed the Social Security numbers and other personal data of more than 200 former congressional staffers and other former officials, including at least two still-living individuals identified in press reporting: Joseph diGenova (Trump's own former personal attorney) and Christopher Pyle (a former Church Committee investigator). More than 80 additional people with birthdates placing them in their 70s, 80s, or 90s also had SSNs and birthdates exposed. Asked about the disclosure, Trump told reporters, 'We even released Social Security numbers, I didn't want anything deleted' -- a direct, on-the-record statement that the unredacted release, including the SSN exposure, was his personal instruction rather than a lower-level processing error. NARA and the Social Security Administration said they were working to identify and contact affected individuals; diGenova said he intended to sue NARA, stating 'They violated the Privacy Act.'
elements_required: A federal agency (NARA) disclosed protected personal records -- Social Security numbers -- of identifiable living individuals without their consent

The disclosure was not required by the underlying declassification mandate; NARA's own established review process for JFK Records Act releases was specifically designed to withhold this category of personal data of living people, and that process was bypassed
The official ordering the release is on the record confirming the unredacted release, including SSN exposure, was intentional and not accidental
Documented harm/risk resulted: named living individuals face identity-theft and fraud exposure, and at least one has stated intent to pursue legal action

comeback: The transparency goal doesn't require exposing living people's current Social Security numbers -- NARA had an established, working redaction process for exactly this category of harm under the same statute, and chose to bypass it under an artificial 24-hour rush that served no disclosure deadline actually set by law. Trump's own on-the-record comment ('I didn't want anything deleted') confirms the SSN exposure was a deliberate choice, not an inadvertent byproduct of a legitimate process.

MODERATE confidence on the ultimate legal characterization (Privacy Act violation) -- a former DHS chief privacy officer and diGenova himself have both characterized it that way, but no court ruling or agency IG finding had resolved the question as of last verification.
